papers.title: Hot Molecular Hydrogen in Galaxies at Redshift ~ 0.2-1.5 Revealed by JWST
papers.abstract: Molecular hydrogen (H$_2$) is the fundamental component of the molecular gas reservoir that fuels star formation and black hole growth. While prominent hot H$_2$ emission ($\gtrsim 1000$ K) has been explored in nearby galaxies, its excitation mechanisms at higher redshifts remain poorly constrained. We present a systematic study of hot molecular gas traced via ro-vibrational H$_2$ emitters at z~0.2-1.5 using JWST slitless spectroscopy. Exploiting JWST's great sensitivity to near-infrared H$_2$ ro-vibrational transitions such as H$_2$ 1-0 S(1), we build a sample of 144 H$_2$-luminous galaxies and characterize their multi-wavelength properties. About 96.5% and 80% of these galaxies are detected in the radio and far-infrared (FIR) bands, respectively, and their hot H$_2$ emission strongly correlates with the radio and FIR radiation. Based on radio excess, X-ray emission, and optical diagnostics, 62 sources (43%) exhibit significant AGN activity. The H$_2$ line luminosities of the sample show a sublinear dependence on radio luminosity, while the relation between the H$_2$ luminosities and total infrared luminosities is approximately linear after excluding the radio-excess sources. These scaling relations suggest that star formation provides a baseline contribution to hot H$_2$ excitation, while radio-excess sources require an additional contribution from AGN-related processes such as jet- or wind-driven shocks. These results reveal a multi-channel excitation scenario and shed new light on the interplay between star formation, AGN activity, and the interstellar medium during galaxy evolution.

papers.title: Large-scale Environmental Dependence of AGN Activity Revealed by JWST Pa$α$ Emitters
papers.abstract: The role of the large-scale environment in regulating AGN activity remains an open question. We investigate the Mpc-scale environments of 70 AGNs at $z=1.1$-$1.5$ using a highly complete sample of 3,419 Pa$α$ emitters with accurate spectroscopic redshifts from JWST slitless spectroscopic survey. This dataset allows us to robustly trace the environments and quantify the environmental dependence of AGN properties. We measure the eighth-nearest-neighbor surface density of Pa$α$ emitters around each AGN, probing $\sim$1.5 pMpc scale environments. We find that this environmental density exhibits a weak positive correlation with radio luminosity. Radio-bright AGNs tend to reside in statistically denser environments than their radio-faint counterparts. The environmental density also has a positive correlation with the Eddington ratio and a weak negative correlation with the central black hole mass, implying more efficient black hole accretion in dense environments. We construct Pa$α$ luminosity functions (LFs) in AGN environments and find that they are systematically elevated relative to the field Pa$α$ LF. In addition, their faint-end slopes are shallower, suggesting accelerated galaxy growth and enhanced quenching of star formation. As Pa$α$ emitters trace gas-rich, star-forming galaxies, our results support a scenario in which the large-scale cold gas promotes AGN activity at cosmic noon.

papers.title: Hopfield Networks in Non-volatile Memory
papers.abstract: Many important computational workloads are bound by the performance of the memory system that supplies data to conventional processors. Compute in Memory (CiM) promises to circumvent this bottleneck by performing the processing within the memory. Neural Networks are memory-bound, and a notable example of such is the Hopfield Network. This work explores the design space of non-volatile computing-in-memory (NV-CiM) architectures using an instruction-level simulator to evaluate application mappings and workload-driven architectural adaptations. The exploration examines the resulting design trade-offs and includes theoretical comparisons with representative CPU and GPU architectures.

papers.title: Generalization Analysis of Biased Stochastic Gradient Methods for Minimax Problems
papers.abstract: Minimax optimization refers to a class of optimization problems with some variables to minimize and other variables to maximize. Biased stochastic gradient methods have shown practical success in solving minimax problems to either improve robustness, enhance communication efficiency, or decrease computational costs. These successes motivate a lot of theoretical works to study the convergence of biased stochastic gradient methods, while their generalization analysis remains untouched. In this paper, we present the first framework to study the stability and generalization of biased stochastic gradient methods for minimax problems. We establish a connection between stability and generalization for minimax problems by relaxing the existing bounded gradient assumption to a bounded second moment condition. We then introduce a generalized Lipschitz-type condition on bias and gradient estimators, and derive a general stability bound to clarify the connection among bias, gradient estimators, and stability. We apply our general analysis to Zeroth-order and Clipped stochastic gradient descent ascent (SGDA), and derive stability bounds that match those of SGDA under appropriate smoothing/clipping parameters. We combine stability and convergence analyses together, and derive optimal excess risk bounds of order $1/\sqrt{n}$, where $n$ is the sample size.

papers.title: TopicMerge: A Divide and Conquer Approach to Topic Modeling
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in topic modeling have split into two main paths: efficient embedding-based methods that offer scalability but are often outperformed on standard clustering metrics, and Large Language Model (LLM) approaches that achieve state-of-the-art clustering performance but at the cost of prohibitive computational expense and poor scalability. This paper introduces TopicMerge, a novel multi-stage pipeline that bridges these approaches to achieve both state-of-the-art clustering performance and computational efficiency. TopicMerge first employs an efficient clustering pipeline to deliberately over-segment a document corpus into a large set of fine-grained, semantically pure micro-clusters, which are then given initial semantic labels. It then introduces a novel, iterative merging algorithm where an LLM, guided by local neighborhood context, arbitrates on consolidating candidate pairs. These approved merges are then selectively executed and semantically relabeled by the LLM, hierarchically building broader, more coherent topics. Extensive experiments on the Bills and Wiki datasets show that TopicMerge achieves state-of-the-art clustering performance while reducing required LLM calls by over 92% compared to document-level methods, offering a practical and scalable solution.

papers.title: Why don't Graph Transformers attend to the same token?
papers.abstract: In large language models (LLMs), attention concentrates heavily on the first token. This 'attention sink' is believed to protect deep models against over-mixing. Even though graph transformers face a related pressure, we find that a SoTA graph transformer, GRIT, rarely forms sinks on molecules, and that it sinks less when trained on larger graphs, the opposite of the trend in LLMs. In principle, a graph can prevent sinks: we prove and show empirically that its symmetry and locality limit the attention any node can receive. On molecules, however, with distinguishable atoms and global attention, neither limit prevents sinks; what stops them lies in the model. We find that the attention scoring function is the main cause. Replacing GRIT's gated logit with a dot product raises its sink rate from 0.09 to 0.68 on identical graphs. In Graph Transformers using dot-product attention, removing the sink gives about the same error as removing a random node, while GRIT's most-attended nodes matter to its predictions. Attention sinks are therefore a property of dot-product attention rather than of Transformers. In our experiments, they form when dot-product scoring has a distinguishable node to concentrate on.

papers.title: AutoPoly-HE: Autonomous Design of Polynomial Activations for Privacy-Preserving Encrypted Inference
papers.abstract: Privacy-preserving machine learning has become critical for deploying artificial intelligence in sensitive domains such as healthcare, finance, and infrastructure monitoring. Homomorphic encryption (HE) enables secure inference on encrypted data. Despite its advantages, HE is not compatible with nonlinear activation functions found in machine learning models. Existing methods mitigate this problem by manually designing polynomial approximations for these activation functions. However, these functions do not account for the differences in dataset characteristics or model architecture. Furthermore, these functions are also limited to the accuracies of convolutional neural network (CNN) models. In this work, we propose an autonomous framework that selects polynomial activation functions tailored to each dataset and model. Using this framework, we analyze the interdependence between polynomial activation design and model architecture by evaluating several CNN ResNet and Vision Transformer models across multiple datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework generalizes across multiple architectures, including ResNet-18, ResNet-34, ResNet-50, ViT-S/16, ViT-B/16, and ViT-L/16. Across all datasets, transformer-based models maintain higher accuracy under polynomial approximation, while convolutional models exhibit increased degradation as task complexity grows. In addition, latency analysis reveals that the proposed CLS token based inference pipeline significantly reduces computational overhead by eliminating depth-dependent operations, shifting the primary cost to encryption and decryption. These findings demonstrate that the proposed method not only adapts polynomial activations across architectures, but also enables efficientencrypted inference through both activation design and pipeline optimization.

papers.title: Solving a sequence of eigenvalue problems using snapshot and row subsampling
papers.abstract: A sequence of eigenvalue problems requires solving $A_i\vec{x}_i= λ_i\vec{x}_i$ where $i \in \{1, \dots, N\}$, $N \gg 1$ and (usually) $λ_i$ is the largest or smallest eigenvalue of $A_i$. Often, the matrices $A_i$ come from a discretization of a smooth map depending on a parameter $p \rightarrow A(p)$, that is $A_i = A(p_i)$, so the matrices $A_i$ change gradually along the sequence. Under this latter assumption, we introduce an efficient algorithm for solving sequences of eigenvalue problems. Our algorithm combines the ideas of reduced order model and row subsampling, as done in [E. Jones and Y. Nakatsukasa, arXiv, 2025] for linear systems. In addition, in our approach, the same set of rows is guaranteed to work well independently of the value of the parameter $p$ or the matrix $A(p)$ as long as the snapshot matrix is unchanged and given that the row subset was chosen well at the beginning. Furthermore, we implement an update strategy of the snapshot matrix. Along these results, we present theoretical analysis of the snapshot matrix for eigenvalue problems, showing an exponential decay of the singular values, and we give bounds on the error on eigenvectors for unseen value of the parameter. This analysis generalizes that in [M. Guido, D. Kressner, and P. Ricci, J. Sci. Comput., 2024] and shows that, regardless of the distribution of the snapshot points, the convergence is always (asymptotically) exponential in the number of snapshot points if the function $A(p)$ admits an analytical extension. We further generalize our algorithm for computing largest or smallest singular values and relative singular vectors and to generalized eigenvalue problems. We conclude with numerical results showing the efficiency of our approach.

papers.title: SonoWorld: Towards Interactive Pose-Controllable Ultrasound World Models
papers.abstract: Robotic ultrasound can standardize image acquisition and reduce operator workload and variability, but policy learning remains limited by the lack of realistic, controllable simulation environments. While controllable world models have advanced rapidly in natural-image domains, ultrasound world modeling remains challenging because each frame captures only a cross-section of unobserved 3D anatomy, causing small probe motions to induce large appearance changes. Existing approaches rely on robot-tracked poses and latent-space prediction, but do not directly generate the observations required for interactive control. We propose SonoWorld, a causal ultrasound world model that learns video dynamics from unlabeled clinical videos and grounds them to 6-DoF control using a small set of freehand clinical scans tracked with an EM sensor. SonoWorld is trained in three stages: pretraining a latent-action-conditioned video diffusion model on around 6.9 million unlabeled multi-organ ultrasound frames; grounding the learned video dynamics to metric probe poses with a small EM-tracked thyroid dataset; and applying distribution matching distillation to enable causal, long-horizon autoregressive generation with selectively caching eviction tokens at inference time. We evaluate controllability through pose-following fidelity, round-trip consistency, and axis-specific control under synthetic actions on held-out tracked scans, and further validate it with a user study. In model-based action discrimination, SonoWorld correctly ranks the target-directed probe motion over an equal-magnitude opposite motion in up to 74.8% of trials. To our knowledge, SonoWorld is the first causal, pose-controllable ultrasound world model learned primarily from freehand clinical videos, providing a data-driven interactive environment for robotic ultrasound data acquisition and policy evaluation.

papers.title: ExoEcho: Exoplanet Ephemerides Change Observations. III. A JWST Survey for Transit Timing Variations of 37 Exoplanets
papers.abstract: Transit timing variations (TTVs) provide a powerful probe of planetary dynamics and orbital evolution. We extend the ExoEcho project by incorporating James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) transit observations and analyze 84 light curves of 37 exoplanets, including 20 hot Jupiters, 11 Neptune-like planets, and 6 super-Earths. We derive updated transit ephemerides and conduct a systematic search for long-term and periodic TTV signals. We identify two strong TTV candidates, including HATS-6~b and HAT-P-18~b. The hot Jupiter HATS-6~b exhibits a long-term trend with $\dot{P} = 230.5 \pm 46.8\ \mathrm{ms\ yr^{-1}}$, potentially driven by tidal interactions with its host star. In addition, the Neptune-like planet HAT-P-18~b shows periodic TTV signal with amplitude of $92.9 \pm 13.7$~s. We also show that the previously claimed positive period derivative in WASP-121~b is inconsistent with our new transit timing data. Although continued monitoring is required to confirm these findings, our results demonstrate the potential of JWST for high-precision transit timing and extend TTV studies beyond the traditional hot-Jupiter population to lower-mass exoplanets.

papers.title: Search for Sub-Solar Mass Binaries in the First and Second Part of LIGO's Fourth Observing Run O4a-O4b
papers.abstract: The observation of sub-solar mass neutron stars and black holes would signify a new class of astrophysical objects since these systems are not expected to form via standard stellar evolution. We present the first sub-solar mass search for binaries consisting of neutron star or black holes that uses the data from both the second part (O4b) and first part (O4a) of the fourth observing run of the Advanced LIGO detectors. The search covers primary masses 0.1 to 2 $M_\odot$ and secondary masses 0.1 to 1 $M_\odot$. Tidal effects up to $7\times10^5$ are accounted for in extremely low-mass neutron stars. No statistically significant candidates are identified. We place a $90\%$ confidence upper limit on the merger rate $\mathcal{R}_{90}$ for sub-solar mass black holes and neutron stars to be $< 5.2\times10^{2}\,\textrm{Gpc}^{-3}\,\textrm{yr}^{-1}$ for a chirp mass of 0.5 $M_\odot$, a factor $2.2 \times$ lower compared to previous O1-O4a searches. We constrain the effective local dark matter fraction to be $\tilde{f}_\textrm{PBH}<0.6\%$ for $M_{\textrm{PBH}}=0.8 \,M_\odot$, approximately $1.5$ factor improvement to previous O1-O4a constraints. Given our model assumptions, our local dark matter fraction constraints are $2-7$ times lower than the OGLE microlensing survey for $M_{\textrm{PBH}}\ge{0.6}~M_\odot$.

papers.title: NavAble: A Large-Scale Dataset and Synthetic Data Generation Pipeline for Blind Navigation
papers.abstract: Reliable recognition of accessibility-critical objects (e.g., audible pedestrian signals, door-activation buttons, and handrails) is essential for assistive navigation technologies that support safe, independent mobility for blind and low-vision (BLV) users. Yet these categories are underrepresented in existing large-scale vision datasets, and the few datasets that include them suffer from limited class coverage, inconsistent annotations, and poor diversity. We introduce NavAble, a large-scale dataset spanning 11 accessibility-critical object classes, combining 41K curated open-source images with 8K newly collected, densely annotated real-world images. To extend scale and diversity, we develop a synthetic data generation pipeline that renders high-fidelity 3D assets across 37 environments under diverse styles and viewpoints, yielding 452K frames with rich ground-truth annotations from 565 assets. The pipeline minimizes manual effort by combining automated web image crawling, VLM-based filtering, SAM 3D-based asset generation, and convenient camera trajectory configuration, enabling large-scale data generation at a diversity unattainable through manual collection. Experiments show that fine-tuning existing segmentation models on the NavAble Dataset achieves reliable accessibility-object segmentation (>80% mIoU on our held-out test set). We also demonstrate the effectiveness of synthetic data augmentation, which yields up to +3.5 mIoU over real-world-only fine-tuning. Beyond benchmark evaluation, validation on egocentric data from two mobility-assistive robots demonstrates improved perception reliability in real-world navigation scenarios. Together, NavAble establishes a scalable foundation for BLV navigation perception, directly addressing the data scarcity and embodiment gaps. The dataset and pipeline are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/NavAble/NeurIPS_2026_BLV.

papers.title: A polylogarithmic bound for list replicability
papers.abstract: Zhang [Zha26] recently posted a manuscript announcing that the list-replicability number of every class of $M\ge 2$ binary concepts on $N\ge 2$ domain points is $O(\log^2 M\log N)$, which would be the first polylogarithmic upper bound on this quantity. In this note, we present a short, self-contained proof of this bound, following the high-level approach of the manuscript but with considerably simpler arguments.

papers.title: LLM-jp-4 Technical Report
papers.abstract: This paper presents LLM-jp-4, a family of Japanese sovereign large language models (LLMs) developed with an emphasis on transparency, reproducibility, and practical usability. LLM-jp-4 comprises an 8B dense model and a 32B-A3B mixture-of-experts model, both trained from scratch on approximately 12 trillion tokens. To support independent verification and reproduction, we establish explicit criteria for selecting training data, external models, and software, and make the development process publicly available. Evaluation results demonstrate substantial improvements over previous LLM-jp models and competitive performance against open-weight models of similar scale. By documenting the development principles, training procedures, and empirical findings of LLM-jp-4, we aim to provide a reference for future sovereign AI development.

papers.title: Nondegeneracy and asymptotic behavior of type I blow-up for semilinear heat equations with general nonlinearities
papers.abstract: We study the local asymptotic behavior of nonnegative type I blow-up solutions to semilinear heat equations with nonlinearities that need not be scale invariant. Using a quasi-similarity transformation adapted to the associated ordinary differential equation, we establish locally uniform convergence to a constant profile on the parabolic spatial scale near every interior blow-up point. Under a quantitative assumption on the nonlinearity at infinity, our results cover regularly varying nonlinearities in the Sobolev subcritical and critical ranges and, in one and two space dimensions, rapidly growing nonlinearities including double exponentials. A key ingredient in this analysis is a positive lower bound for the normalized solution at interior blow-up points. In fact, under weaker assumptions on the nonlinearity, we prove this bound in arbitrary space dimension without assuming radial symmetry.

papers.title: Algebraic overtwistedness of contact $(+1)$-surgeries via augmented Floer theories
papers.abstract: We prove that contact $(+1)$-surgery along a Legendrian $n$-sphere $Λ\subset(\mathbb{S}^{2n+1},ξ_{\mathrm{std}})$ with \[ \mathrm{tb}(Λ)\ne (-1)^{\frac{n(n-1)}{2}+1} \] has vanishing contact homology. In dimension three, this produces new examples of tight algebraically overtwisted contact manifolds, vastly extending the authors' previous results: If a Legendrian knot in $(\mathbb{S}^3,ξ_{\mathrm{std}})$ admits an exact, oriented Lagrangian filling that is not a disk, then contact $(+1/k)$-surgery on it is algebraically overtwisted and tight for every positive integer $k$. Our proofs use versions of symplectic cohomology and wrapped Floer cohomology defined by augmentations of a chain-level contact homology algebra.

papers.title: Evidence for hidden order and its potential correlation with electron-hole asymmetry in iridate superlattices
papers.abstract: Hidden order refers to an order that shapes the properties of quantum materials yet remains difficult to identify. Here we report signatures of a hidden order in doped iridate superlattices through an unexpected electron-hole asymmetry in the coupling between the insulating state and the antiferromagnetic (AFM) state. While carrier doping suppresses both states, they remain coupled in the electron-doped regime but decouple in the hole-doped regime. Structural analysis rules out octahedral rotation and tilting as the dominant origin of this asymmetry. Instead, magnetic characterization reveals evidences of a hidden order that only appears in the hole-doped regime. This hidden order emerges above TN and is closely associated with the AFM state, coinciding with an exceptionally strong magnetic scattering intensity and an anomalously robust magnetic coherence. Our results highlight that hole-doped iridates can be a promising platform for exploring hidden and unconventional ordering phenomena in spin-orbit-entangled quantum materials.

papers.title: Differentially Private Learning of Markov Chains: Near-Optimal Sample Complexity for Item and User Level Privacy
papers.abstract: Sequential data such as documents, conversations, and trajectories are naturally partitioned across users, motivating privacy guarantees that protect each user's entire trajectory. We initiate the study of privately estimating the transition matrix of a discrete ergodic Markov chain from N independent trajectories of length T, with arbitrary initial distributions, under maximum row-wise ell 1 error. Besides N, T, and the number of states, our bounds depend on the minimum stationary probability and the pseudo-spectral gap, which govern state coverage and mixing. Under item-level privacy, we give upper and lower bounds that separate the costs of sampling, state occupancy and mixing, and privacy. Under user-level privacy, we reduce the problem for sufficiently long trajectories to private product distribution estimation. Along the way, we establish optimal user-level private bounds for estimating products of discrete distributions, which may be of independent interest. In the user level setting, our bounds are nearly tight in the large T regime, whereas in the item-level setting, our bounds as tight up-to a non-private term.

papers.title: Probabilistic Physics Digital Twin for Human-Robot Interaction
papers.abstract: Digital twins are increasingly used in robotics to simulate interactions, predict action outcomes, and support planning. However, constructing accurate digital twins requires precise estimates of physical properties such as mass, friction, and center of mass, which are often difficult to obtain in real-world environments. We propose probabilistic digital twins, which represent uncertain physical properties as probability distributions rather than fixed values. By simulating actions across these distributions, the twin predicts a range of possible outcomes and their likelihoods. These probabilistic simulations can guide both human and robot actions by identifying actions that are effective despite physical uncertainty. We demonstrate this framework through human-robot interaction scenarios, including interfaces that communicate simulated outcomes to users and robot planning strategies that explicitly account for uncertainty.

papers.title: Beyond Initial Creation: Two Decades of Community-based Chart Revisions from Wikimedia Commons
papers.abstract: Open online communities like Wikipedia offer a rich space for understanding the organic evolution of public-facing artifacts, but little is known about how these communities collectively edit chart images. We investigate the phenomenon of "community editing" of visualizations by exploring chart revision patterns on Wikimedia Commons. We introduce a novel dataset of 7,786 longitudinal chart revisions across 1,664 images, labeled with edit categories using an LLM pipeline. Initial data analysis uncovered several novel findings. Multi-contributor revision is associated with more edits to mark styling and text content compared to single-contributor revision. Temporally, mark and text edits occur in more "bursty" cadences than data edits. In addition, while SVG charts attract more unique contributors and revisions than raster charts, their edit histories involve more tightly scoped and less diverse changes. This dataset enables a wide range of analyses of chart change over time.

papers.title: The Gompertz-Zipf city size distribution and urban allometry
papers.abstract: This dissertation discusses the distribution of city sizes using censuses of the Brazilian Institute for Geography and Statistics (IBGE) spanning 150 years, from 1872 to 2022, as well as the allometric scaling relation with the 2022 census data. The Gompertz distribution is fitted to the population size of less populated cities, while the Zipf power law is used to represent the cities having larger populations, with threshold varying between 20,216 and 102,857 inhabitants. The data analysis shows that the Gompertz-Zipf distribution can describe the data across all censuses, with the Gompertz parameter $B$ oscillating between $-2.39\times10^{-5}$ and $-1.49\times10^{-5}$, indicating periods with faster decreases and periods with slower decreases in the number of cities within the less populated segment as population increases, while the Zipf exponent ranges from $a=3.61\pm0.09$ in 1872 to $a=2.28\pm0.02$ in 2022. The Gini coefficient $G$ and the Zanardi index $Z$ are used to quantify the inequality in the city population distribution, whose obtained values are $G=0.439$ and $Z=-0.002$ for the 1872 census and $G=0.733$ and $Z=0.018$ for the 2022 dataset, while the Pietra index $p$ and the Kolkata index $k$, associated with the most populated cities, are $p=31.893\%$ and $k=65.894\%$ for 1872, and $p=57.395\%$ and $k=78.342\%$ for 2022. These results reveal a high concentration of population in larger cities, with $G$ increasing from 1872 to 2022 and $Z$ becoming positive after 1900, indicating a greater concentration of population in the group of more populated cities than in the group of less populated cities. Finally, urban allometry is also examined, generating an exponent $b=0.835$ for the 2022 data, showing that the scaling relation between area and population holds for urbanized area but not for total administrative area, indicating that scaling is associated with spatial occupation.

papers.title: Can We Believe AI Peer Review?
papers.abstract: As large language models become widely used in scientific review and manuscript revision, AI scores are increasingly serving as feedback for assessing paper quality and guiding edits. Yet whether a single AI score reliably reflects the reviewer's judgment, and whether revision gains based on that score are endorsed by other reviewers, remain understudied. Using 200 papers from ICLR 2025 and 2026 and approximately 14,000 AI reviews, we study score reliability, score-distribution estimation, and cross-model agreement on revision gains. Repeated reviews fluctuate even under identical conditions. Finer-grained scoring protocols reduce score variance but also systematically shift mean scores, while the gains assigned to manuscript revisions depend strongly on the reviewer.

papers.title: Uniqueness of Limit Cycles for Abel Equations and Planar Systems
papers.abstract: We study positive limit cycles of the Abel equation $$\dot{x}=A(t)x^{3}+B(t)x^{2},$$ where $A$ and $B$ are $2π$-periodic functions. By developing a half-period convexity method, we establish a new criterion ensuring that the equation has at most one positive limit cycle. Moreover, if such a limit cycle exists, it is hyperbolic. As applications, we consider two classes of planar polynomial systems that can be reduced to Abel equations. For a subfamily of cubic rigid systems, we prove that there is at most one limit cycle, thereby giving a partial answer to the first problem in Gasull's list of 33 open problems. For quadratic systems, we derive a new uniqueness criterion for limit cycles surrounding the origin and provide explicit parameter regions under which the criterion is satisfied.

papers.title: MMKG-R1: Constructing Multimodal Knowledge Graphs via Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Multimodal knowledge graphs (MMKGs) organize information across different modalities to support multimodal Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), which aims to improve the performance of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). The effectiveness of these multimodal Graph RAG methods largely depends on the quality of the constructed MMKGs. However, most existing methods construct MMKGs without explicit guidance on graph quality, while reinforcement learning (RL)-based methods that rely on final-answer correctness may provide only indirect feedback on MMKG quality. To address these limitations, we propose MMKG-R1, a novel MMKG-quality-driven RL framework for training an MLLM as a multimodal knowledge constructor. To be specific, MMKG-R1 introduces multiple quality-aware rewards to directly evaluate both the quality of information extracted from individual knowledge sources and the quality of the assembled MMKG. These rewards are then used to guide the RL training. Experiments across multiple datasets show that MMKG-R1 constructs MMKGs that improve downstream question-answering accuracy.

papers.title: Why Do Agent Teams Fail Across Boundaries? A Failure Taxonomy for Agent-to-Agent Systems with Private States
papers.abstract: Agents are increasingly interacting with other agents that act for different principals (people or organizations on whose behalf they work), such as a buyer's personal agent negotiating with an enterprise's seller agent. In such agent-to-agent (A2A) scenarios, each agent has its own environment and holds information and authority that the other cannot see. Moreover, the interests of each agent may be aligned (cooperative), partly aligned (mixed-motive), or opposed (competitive). Existing multi-agent system failure studies assume one orchestrator, shared workspace, or single principal. We ask how A2A systems fail when these assumptions are removed. We study more than 2,500 recorded runs of A2A systems built from different agent harnesses and models, spanning 488 scenarios across eight families (legal, CRM, security, commerce, etc.). From these traces, we derive $A^2$-Failures, a taxonomy of 20 A2A failure modes in four categories: (i) discovery and delegation, (ii) grounding and record consistency, (iii) verification, and (iv) conduct and fidelity. Three findings hold across every harness, model, and scenario studied: (1) discovery and interaction are driven by the phrasing of the task rather than the availability of peer agents; (2) no agent verifies a peer's factual claim on its own initiative, so an A2A system inherits the reliability of its least reliable participant unless the protocol or mechanism performs the check; and (3) the aggregate outcome score credits the agent completing the task while staying blind to the coordination, verification, and conduct failures beneath it, so A2A systems must be evaluated per agent, against each agent's own principal. We release the run logs behind the taxonomy at https://huggingface.co/datasets/a2a-salesforce/a2-failures.

papers.title: Counterfactual Gate-Support Decomposition: Separating Selection from Redistribution in Training-Data Filtering
papers.abstract: A training-data quality gate changes both which examples survive within regions of the input space and how training mass is distributed across those regions, so a gate-versus-random comparison does not isolate these mechanisms. We introduce Counterfactual Gate-Support Decomposition (CGSD), a four-arm, budget-matched design that crosses gate eligibility with support distribution and decomposes the observed gate effect into within-support selection, between-support redistribution, and their interaction. The practical constraint is finite-pool realizability: we characterize mass and token-assembly conditions under which the required arms can be constructed, together with a support-extinction case in which the ordinary design is undefined. On Korean-English and Korean-Japanese retrieval, the mean within-support selection component is the only one that exceeds its calibrated null band (+29.7 and +5.6 holdout items; 30/30 positive replicates), decisively in Korean-English and marginally in Korean-Japanese; redistribution and interaction remain unresolved at the available power. The same pattern holds for a second, unrelated gate family -- a model-confidence threshold rather than a deterministic verifier -- judged against its own null (+27.3 items, 9/9 positive), so the result is not a property of one gate's mechanism. On a mathematics gate, zero-eligibility supports leave the ordinary design undefined at every budget, while the extended design is constructible only inside narrow budget bands that an exhaustive scan locates and that the natural operating point misses -- the assembly condition separating a property of the pool from a limitation of the packer. CGSD therefore returns a decomposition, a constructible-but-underpowered design, or an explicit non-constructibility result, and says which; it prevents support redistribution from being silently interpreted as sample-level gate quality.

papers.title: Target-Token Asymmetry Can Masquerade As Depth Specialization
papers.abstract: Layer-ablation studies often perturb early or late layers of a language model, compare the damage to prediction on two corpora, and read a larger early-layer effect on one corpus as early-layer specialization for its task. Such a comparison averages over the tokens that each corpus asks the model to predict, and these target tokens differ: math solutions, for example, ask for far more whitespace and numbers than encyclopedia prose. We show that this difference can create the appearance of depth specialization. We split a cross-corpus early--late damage interaction by target-token type and recompute it under a target mixture shared by both corpora. Between GSM8K and Wikitext, a positive interaction replicates across five model instances. In the three fully decomposed models, only whitespace has a positive interaction. Removing whitespace reverses the pooled effect in all three, and matching the full target mixture reverses it in two. The diagnosis holds under position matching, adversarial reassignment of token types, and a continuous readout. The risk can also be anticipated from the tokenizer alone. A screen computed before any model runs places every held-out pair it scored in the region its label predicts, and on the pairs it rates at high or medium risk, removing whitespace reverses every positive pooled estimate. A smaller content-word effect one token ahead follows the share of content targets that the unablated model already predicts. A cross-corpus depth effect therefore supports an interpretation of task specialization only after the target-token mixture is reported, the effect is decomposed by token type, and a mixture-matched summary keeps its sign.

papers.title: When Is Smaller Greener? Right-Sizing Language Models for Agentic AI
papers.abstract: AI agents use a large language model (LLM) to plan and act over many steps. Which model should an agent use, so that its tasks are completed reliably with the least energy, cost and time? We treat this as a multi-criteria decision problem in which comparisons per call can mislead: a task succeeds only if all its steps succeed, and failed attempts still use resources. We therefore compare models on resources per successfully completed task. We derive crossover task lengths at which two models exchange their efficiency ranking, determined by their per-step reliability and resource use. Each objective has its own crossover. Below the shortest crossover the less reliable model dominates, above the longest the more reliable one dominates, and in between both are Pareto-efficient and preferences decide. This supports a two-stage framework: a preference-free dominance screen, followed by a multi-criteria ranking of the efficient models, subject to reliability and feasibility constraints. We also give conditions under which this structure holds when reliability and resource use change during a task. In a pilot with 15 open-weight models on two synthetic agent tasks, with measured GPU energy, the predicted crossover fell within the observed range for 72 of the 88 observed crossovers. At 20 steps, a 3-billion-parameter model used a tenth of the energy of a 27-billion one per completed task; at 100 steps, a 1.7-billion model used almost four times as much as an 8-billion one. Smaller is greener only up to a task length that can be predicted.

papers.title: Combined Absorption and Emission Study of Air Species in NASA EAST
papers.abstract: A suite of tunable diode laser absorption spectroscopy (TDLAS) diagnostics targeting rovibrational states of nitric oxide (NO) in the mid-infrared (MIR) and electronic states of atomic oxygen (O) and nitrogen (N) in the near-IR (NIR) was combined with optical emission spectroscopy (OES) for overlapping wavelengths at the NASA Electric Arc Shock Tube (EAST) facility for three selected high-temperature air experiments. Absorption features were probed at rates up to 1 MHz to provide quantitative, time-resolved measurements of temperature and species number density profiles behind incident shocks, enabling comparisons to spatially-resolved emission measurements, with the two typically agreeing within their respective uncertainties. Inferred time-histories are further compared to incident shock simulations from two one-dimensional models - one leveraging the Park two-temperature rates and the other more recent rate values - as well as the Data Parallel Line Relaxation (DPLR) code. For the two low-velocity cases (3.81 and 3.98 km/s) in which NO is probed, inferred temperatures are typically well-captured by all three models, although the NO number densities show stronger variation, agreeing better for the model with updated NO formation and dissociation rates. Finally, one high-velocity case (7.03 km/s) demonstrates the simultaneous resolution of three O-atom and six N-atom electronic states, with all states showing a steady increase in number density over time - possibly due to shock trajectory effects. Together, this combined absorption and emission study demonstrates resolution of many states of nonequilibrium air species, while directly comparing ground- and excited-state populations via the combined diagnostic strategy.

papers.title: Integrated Novelty Detection Systems: From Sensor Networks to Multi-Novelty Computer Vision
papers.abstract: Novelty detection is crucial in various technological and scientific domains. Its importance spans from ensuring the reliability of sensor networks to enhancing the adaptability of computer vision systems. As AI systems become increasingly sophisticated and complex, effective anomaly detection is essential for maintaining reliability and accuracy. This work addresses novelty detection in weather sensor networks and computer vision. In weather sensor networks, particularly for monitoring rainfall, detecting blocked rain gauges can significantly impact data reliability, food security, and disaster management. This work evaluates four existing quality control methods for detecting blocked rain gauges and demonstrates their limitations, particularly in detecting clusters of faulty sensors. By comparing methods such as the Conditional Mixture Model (CMM), PSWQ (Fz-filter), Kernel Regression, and Gaussian Method, we identify their shortcomings and propose three novel quality control techniques that integrate probabilistic fault detection and consistency-based diagnosis framework to improve timely detection of blocked sensors, while reducing false alarms. In the realm of computer vision, current systems often fail to handle multiple types of novelty due to their focus on single-novelty scenarios. We highlight the need for integrated systems capable of handling multiple types of novelty. To support this, we introduce the Novel Snapshot Serengeti (NOVEL-SS) dataset, derived from the Snapshot Serengeti camera trap data, which includes various forms of novelty. We also present the DCA (Detect, Characterize, and Accommodate) baseline system, designed to handle multiple novelty by detecting, characterizing, and accommodating them. This work aims to advance the robustness and adaptability of novelty detection systems across both weather sensor networks and computer vision applications.

papers.title: Magnetic Reconnection Governs the Entire Lifecycle of Solar Eruptive Magnetic Flux Rope
papers.abstract: While magnetic flux ropes (MFRs) are widely accepted to exist prior to many solar eruptions, the physical mechanism responsible for triggering and subsequently driving their eruptions remains debated. Classical models commonly attribute eruption onset to ideal magnetohydrodynamic instabilities, particularly the torus instability, while magnetic reconnection is often regarded as a secondary process. Using high-resolution three-dimensional MHD simulations, we investigate the eruption of an MFR that forms self-consistently through flux cancellation driven by converging motions and photospheric diffusion following an initial shearing phase. The pre-eruption MFR rises quasi-statically and reaches a height where the decay index exceeds the classical torus instability threshold, yet the system continues to evolve quasi-statically without eruption. Instead, eruption begins only when the current sheet beneath the MFR becomes sufficiently thin for magnetic reconnection to set in. Increasing numerical resolution systematically delays the eruption onset, whereas the decay index at eruption onset remains nearly unchanged, demonstrating that the onset is governed by reconnection rather than torus instability. During the eruption, magnetic reconnection continuously converts surrounding sheared arcades into newly reconnected twisted flux that merges with the pre-eruption MFR and continuously to build the erupting MFR. A component-resolved analysis of the Lorentz force work further shows that the newly reconnection flux contributes predominantly to the main acceleration phase. These results demonstrate that magnetic reconnection plays a central role throughout the entire lifecycle of the eruptive MFR: it builds the MFR, directly triggers its eruption, and provides the dominant driving of the eruption.

papers.title: Where to Start, How to Move: Analyzing Curricula under GRPO for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) provides no reward-relative learning signal when all rollouts receive identical rewards. In long-horizon tasks that require multiple interactions, rewards are given only upon successful task completion, making all-fail groups common early in training and limiting opportunities to practice later steps. Guide Assisted GRPO replays a successful reference prefix before the learner continues. We study how initial positions, handoff units, and movement rules affect unassisted task completion. Across three model sizes on BFCL, starting near completion is more effective under a fixed turn-level threshold rule. Finer handoffs alone do not consistently help, but outcome-informed tool-call selection outperforms GRPO on trained and untrained task categories. Guided starts also improve AppWorld success on both evaluation splits. These findings highlight where learning starts and how starting positions move as key curriculum choices.

papers.title: On Local Inference for Functionals of Ill-Posed Inverse Problems
papers.abstract: We study inference for continuous linear functionals of solutions to ill-posed inverse problems, including Euclidean parameters arising in nonparametric instrumental variables, proximal causal inference, and shadow-variable models. Although pointwise root-$n$ inference is possible under standard conditions, we show that this need not translate into locally reliable inference. Under a model imposing only minimal regularity conditions, the target is Hellinger discontinuous when both inverse problems are ill-posed: arbitrarily small changes in the data-generating law can produce arbitrarily large changes in the target, ruling out informative locally uniform inference. Imposing a uniform bound on a minimum-norm solution restores Hellinger continuity under regularity conditions, but does not by itself ensure stable root-n inference. If, in addition, both inverse problems are ill-posed and the solution whose norm is uniformly bounded is nonunique at a law $P_0$, then under regularity conditions the target fails to be pathwise differentiable; consequently, asymptotically linear estimators exhibit nonvanishing root-$n$ bias under some local alternatives, causing Wald confidence intervals to undercover asymptotically. Under regularity conditions, pathwise differentiability is restored if the uniformly bounded solution is unique at $P_0$. It is also restored, regardless of uniqueness, under the stronger requirement that the corresponding solution satisfy a uniformly bounded $β$-source condition for some $β$>0. We relate these regimes to very weak, weak, and strong identification in instrumental variables models.

papers.title: Subdata Selection for Measurement-Constrained Linear Regression under Model Misspecification
papers.abstract: In many modern applications, obtaining response variables is costly, time-consuming, or technically challenging, making it impractical to measure outcomes for all available units. In such settings, covariates may be available for a large pool of candidates, but responses can only be collected for a small, carefully selected subset, making the choice of which units to measure a consequential decision. Most existing subsampling methods are developed for massive datasets, emphasizing the trade-off between statistical accuracy and computational cost, and typically relying on the assumption of a correctly specified model. These features limit their suitability in measurement-constrained settings, where statistical efficiency is paramount and model misspecification is often unavoidable. To address these challenges, we develop a new subset selection framework for linear regression that accommodates potential model misspecification. The proposed approach targets predictive expected loss and yields an A-optimality-type criterion that depends only on covariate information, requiring no response observations at the selection stage. We refer to this method as Expected Loss Optimal Selection (ELOS). By focusing on predictive risk rather than model-based optimality, ELOS remains well-defined and robust under misspecification. Simulation studies and real data applications demonstrate that ELOS achieves strong predictive performance and compares favorably with existing methods across a range of scenarios.

papers.title: BFHD: Bidirectional Feature Harmonization Decomposition for Heterogeneous Clinical Assessments
papers.abstract: Clinical assessments are often collected using heterogeneous assessment systems across centers and time, leading to records that mix different but related sets of measurements. This motivates harmonization beyond total-score linking. We formulate clinical harmonization at the measurement level as a bidirectional recoverability problem: given paired observations from two assessment systems, the goal is to identify which measurements can be reliably translated in both directions within an application-defined tolerance, while separating non-translatable components. We propose Bidirectional Feature Harmonization Decomposition (BFHD), a feasibility-driven framework that enforces bidirectionally coupled translation and uses feature-wise output gating to produce an explicit decomposition in the original measurement space. Experiments on synthetic data and real clinical assessment pairs show that BFHD achieves broader feasible harmonization coverage and improved subset stability compared to baselines.

papers.title: Longitudinal Brain Aging in Covariance Space: Temporally Calibrated Bayesian Inference for Adaptive Covariance Operators
papers.abstract: Functional brain aging is often characterized by differences between people of different ages, although aging unfolds within individuals. This distinction is especially important for functional connectivity, where the direction of covariance change may evolve across adulthood. We introduce a Bayesian longitudinal covariance-operator framework that models each visit covariance as a latent positive-definite state informed by repeated resting-state fMRI runs. The approach calibrates run-level information for temporal dependence and replicate variability, separates within-person aging from between-person age differences, and uses an adaptive tangent representation to learn the low-dimensional structure of longitudinal change without relying on pooled covariance variation. The longitudinal operator varies smoothly in magnitude and orientation with age, while exact Fréchet derivatives translate the fitted trajectory to the covariance scale. This framework allows us to examine how brain covariance organization changes within individuals, whether longitudinal aging follows the population age gradient, and which functional systems contribute to their divergence. In the Dallas Lifespan Brain Study, within-person covariance aging differs substantially from the cross-sectional age gradient through early and middle adulthood, with the discrepancy diminishing later in life. Covariance reorganization is strongest around midlife, and the longitudinal signal is concentrated in a few coordinated directions, with most off-diagonal change occurring between functional systems. These findings demonstrate that population-level signatures of brain aging do not necessarily reflect individual aging trajectories and highlight the importance of modeling longitudinal covariance change directly.

papers.title: Discrete Edge Multiscale Space based Hybrid Schwarz Preconditioner for High-Frequency Helmholtz Problems
papers.abstract: In this work, we develop a novel hybrid Schwarz method, termed as edge multiscale space based hybrid Schwarz (EMs-HS), for solving the Helmholtz problem with large wavenumbers. The problem is discretized using $H^1$-conforming nodal finite element methods on meshes of size $h$ decreasing faster than $k^{-3/2}$ such that the discretization error can be bounded by the data uniformly with respect to $k$. EMs-HS consists of a one-level Schwarz preconditioner (RAS-imp) and a coarse solver in a multiplicative way. The RAS-imp preconditioner solves local problems on overlapping subdomains with impedance boundary conditions in parallel, and combines the local solutions using partition of unity. On the PDE level, this coarse space corresponds to an edge multiscale space proposed in {[S. Fu, G. Li, R. Craster, and S. Guenneau, \emph{Multiscale Model. Simul.}, 19(4):1684-1709, 2021]}. The approximation properties of this coarse space to the discrete solutions from the primal and adjoint problems are derived by a novel conforming Galerkin finite element method based upon a nonstandard variational formulation. This work represents the first theoretical analysis of an edge multiscale space at the discrete level. We prove that the EMs-HS preconditioner leads to a convergent fixed-point iteration uniformly for large wavenumbers, by rigorously analyzing the approximation properties of the coarse space to the global Helmholtz harmonic extension part and to the solution of the adjoint problem. We provide extensive numerical results on the sharpness of the theoretical findings and also demonstrate the method on challenging heterogeneous models.

papers.title: Two non-semisimple quantum invariants of lens spaces
papers.abstract: We calculate the chromatic spherical invariant $\mathscr{K}_{\mathrm{Rep}(H)}(L(p,q))$ of lens spaces $L(p, q)$ for arbitrary finite-dimensional unibalanced, unimodular Hopf algebras $H$. In the case of the index-2 Nichols Hopf algebra $\mathcal{K}_2$ and $q=1$, we find that the invariant of $L(p, 1)$ depends only on the parity of $p$ for $p\geq 1$. We also describe the duals $\mathcal{S_I}(M)^*$ of the admissible skein modules of handlebodies $M=H_g$ and of $M=L(p, q)$ for arbitrary tensor ideals $\mathcal{I}$ of a ribbon tensor category. In particular, $\mathcal{S_I}(L(p, q))^*$ corresponds with cyclic traces on $\mathcal{I}$ satisfying a property reminiscent of the modified trace condition.

papers.title: Fluctuations in the Potts spin glass model at high temperature
papers.abstract: We study the fluctuations of the free energy of the Potts spin glass with $κ$ colors at high temperature. The disorder is symmetric with unit variance and finite fourth moment. For configurations with a balanced, or nearly balanced, color profile, the log-partition function satisfies a central limit theorem whenever $β^2<α_c(κ)$. Here $κα_c(κ)$ is the critical inverse temperature of the Curie-Weiss-Potts model. A comparison of color profiles transfers this limit to the unconstrained model for $β<β_{\max}(κ)$, an explicit threshold. In the same range, the magnetizations of two replicas and their overlap matrix satisfy a joint quenched central limit theorem with independent Gaussian limits. The fourth cumulant of the disorder enters the limiting mean and variance explicitly.

papers.title: On the Arnold corank, the Zariski multiplicity, and the tangent Milnor fiber problems
papers.abstract: In this article, we approach the Arnold corank problem posed by Arnold himself in 1975, which asks whether the corank of a holomorphic function is a topological invariant. Here, the corank of a holomorphic function is the corank of its Hessian matrix at 0, which is one of the most basic and fundamental invariants of a holomorphic function. Here, we prove the topological invariance of the corank mod 2. Consequently, we obtain another proof of the Arnold corank problem in dimension 3, which was recently proved by Fernandes, Jelonek, and the author of this article. We also prove that the corank is constant in a continuous family of holomorphic functions with isolated singularities and constant Milnor number. We also approach a conjecture recently posed by Budur, Fernández de Bobadilla, Lê, and Nguyen (2022), which states that if two germs of holomorphic functions are right topologically equivalent, then the Milnor fibers of their initial forms are homotopy equivalent. We prove that a (much) weaker version of this conjecture, which states that if two holomorphic functions are right topologically equivalent, then the Milnor fibers of their initial forms have the same Euler characteristic, is equivalent to the Zariski multiplicity conjecture for right topological equivalence. Some other results are also presented here. For instance, the multiplicity $> 2$ of generalized semi-Bireskorn-Pham hypersurfaces is an invariant for the right topological equivalence.

papers.title: Asymptotic Behavior of Transformers
papers.abstract: In this paper we study the behavior of transformer networks generating text over long periods of time. We show that even a three-token, single-layer attention-only transformer can fail to converge. We then study a rich class of transformers with arbitrary finite depth, layer normalization, MLPs, RoPE encodings, and an arbitrary mix of local and global layers. Every transformer in this class has a softmax temperature threshold above which its empirical cache distribution converges to a unique limit, independent of initial conditions. We show further that, while each transformer has a temperature threshold, the supremum of this set is infinite, so there is no global minimal temperature that forces all transformers to converge.

papers.title: Steering Vectors for Competing Ethical Frameworks Are Interchangeable: A Competing-Target Test for Activation Steering
papers.abstract: Activation steering adds a vector to a model's hidden states to control a named behaviour. A gain on that behaviour, however, does not show that the vector controls it directly: it may act through a component shared with neighbouring behaviours, which unsteered and random baselines cannot separate. We introduce the competing-target test: a vector is compared with the vector built the same way for a competing target, and an equivalence test states when their difference is below a useful margin. We apply it in open-weight models to vectors for Kantian deontology, which judges an act by the rule it follows, and act utilitarianism, which judges it by the welfare it produces. On held-out situations, prompting a framework raises its score and lowers the other's, whereas vectors for either framework move both scores alike, and none reaches the margin. The two vectors share most of their direction, a request to apply some framework; the same construction separates an optimistic from a pessimistic tone, whose vectors share much less. What a vector shares with its competitors therefore sets what it controls: steering a perspective can deliver a mixture, and measuring a disposition can measure its neighbours, unless tested against the competing target.

papers.title: Poincaré compactifications of pullbacks of parallel vector fields under counterexamples to the real Jacobian conjecture
papers.abstract: Let $F: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be a polynomial map with nowhere zero Jacobian determinant. It is known that the global invertibility of $F$ is equivalent to the pullback of a parallel vector field being parallel. In this paper, we construct the phase portraits on the Poincaré disc of the pullbacks of the canonical annular, radial, and strip vector fields under non-injective maps $F$ that have recently appeared in the literature. Our arguments use local and global properties of vector fields as well as local and global properties of functions, thereby connecting techniques from dynamical systems and singularity theory.

papers.title: VLX-Go: Robust Embodied Tracking through Multi-Stage Learning and On-Policy Refinement
papers.abstract: Embodied visual tracking requires a robot to identify a designated target from visual observations and control its own motion to follow that target through an environment. Following an isolated person is a comparatively simple demonstration of embodied visual tracking, but following the intended person among distractors remains challenging. Existing methods exhibit a substantial drop in success from single-target to distractor tracking, motivating a focus on the shared spaces that person-following robots must navigate. We present VLX-GO, a vision-language waypoint policy built around the hypothesis that visual and language representations should be aligned before tracking-specific motion is learned. The policy combines complementary frozen visual encoders, multiscale temporal context, a transformer backbone, and a lightweight head for robot-centric waypoint prediction. Its training progresses through vision--language alignment, multimodal reasoning mid-training, and tracking specialization on 19,532 oracle episodes. Compared with 41.54% distractor-tracking success for our earlier OmTrackVLA model, the complete multi-stage recipe achieves 55.80%. We then explore on-policy refinement using filtered oracle labels for states visited by the policy. This preliminary study adds 2.42 percentage points of distractor-tracking success, reaching 58.22%, while reducing collision rate by 1.99 pts. The final policy records the highest distractor- and ambiguous-tracking success rates among the compared methods. These results support staged multimodal learning as a promising direction for tracking among distractors and motivate further study of on-policy refinement for person following in shared spaces. Code is available at https://github.com/om-ai-lab/VLX-Go.

papers.title: Tail Competition Explains Scaling in Best-of-N Sampling for Verifiable Problems
papers.abstract: Best-of-N sampling is a simple inference-time scaling strategy for large language models, yet its behavior under incomplete reward models remains poorly understood. We study Best-of-N as a competition between the extreme reward tails of correct and incorrect responses. This view shows that success depends not only on the probability of sampling a correct response, but also on whether correct responses dominate incorrect ones in the upper tail. Using extreme value theory, we characterize three asymptotic regimes: correct-tail-dominant, incorrect-tail-dominant, and critical explaining both monotonic gains and reward-hacking-induced degradation. We further derive finite-sample scaling laws for representative reward distributions, showing that, under Gaussian rewards, incorrect responses with sufficiently large variance can dominate selection even when their mean reward is lower. Unlike oracle selection, convergence with an incomplete selector can be polynomial rather than exponential. Finally, we propose a lightweight tail-tension criterion to estimate when additional sampling may become harmful. Experiments on synthetic data and real reward model scores are consistent with the theoretically predicted regimes, scaling laws, and diagnostic behavior, suggesting that tail competition provides a unified lens on Best-of-N sampling for verifiable problems.

papers.title: Bicolored Eulerian quasisymmetric functions, affine lengths, and Theta operators
papers.abstract: We introduce a $q$-analogue of the bicolored Eulerian quasisymmetric functions by incorporating an additional grading arising from affine length, obtained by interpreting bicolored permutations as affine permutations. We also provide an intrinsic description of this refinement in terms of bicolored permutations by introducing notions of alignments and crossings, together with an explicit bijection identifying these statistics with the alignments and crossings in the existing literature. Finally, we prove that our refinement is symmetric by expressing it in terms of the Theta operators appearing in the Theta coinvariant Conjecture and the modified Macdonald symmetric functions. Assuming the Theta coinvariant conjecture implies the Schur-positivity of our refinement.

papers.title: Dynamic Graph World Modelling: Learning Future Dynamics from Temporal Context
papers.abstract: Dynamic graph learning models how entities and their relations evolve from historical observations to predict future graph states. Existing methods do not fully address dynamic graph world modelling, which requires learning transitions from temporal context to future latent graph states. This is difficult for three reasons: nodes and relations rely on different historical evidence, structural evolution is path-dependent, and future snapshots provide sparse and realization-specific targets. We propose Dynamic Graph World Modelling (DyG-WM), the first framework to jointly predict future node and relation representations from temporal context by answering three questions: what has evolved, how it evolved, and what will evolve next. To capture what has evolved, a historical node-relation context encoder summarizes node-neighborhood trajectories and pair-specific histories. To characterize how it evolved, a node-relation path-signature encoder captures ordered structural changes. To predict what will evolve next, a dual-level joint-embedding objective predicts target-snapshot node and relation representations without reconstructing the raw graph. Experiments on 12 link-prediction and two node-classification datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of DyG-WM across both tasks.

papers.title: DANGERLENS: Probing Dangerous Representations Hidden by Safety Alignment
papers.abstract: Safety alignment teaches language models to refuse harmful requests, yet the internal accessibility of hazardous concepts can retain traces of earlier training. Can checkpoints with equally safe behavior differ in what remains accessible behind their refusals? In this work, we investigate this question through paired training histories and a direct audit of intermediate representations. We introduce DANGERLENS, a probe that maps hidden states into vocabulary space and uses blinded semantic judgments to distinguish harmful goals and operational means from hazard recognition and safety control. Experiments on three Qwen1.5 scales show that checkpoints with prior harmful exposure generally retain greater hazardous concept accessibility after the same safety alignment, with the strongest separation in intermediate and later layers. The same harmful update also produces different behavioral trajectories from closely matched starting points. Human relevance validation and readout ablations reinforce the measured accessibility contrast. Our findings show that training history remains visible inside behaviorally matched models and motivate internal accessibility audits alongside output safety evaluations.

papers.title: Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning: The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory
papers.abstract: Multimodal models and agents have emerged to enable AI systems to learn from and interact with the real world more like humans by integrating information across multiple modalities. However, enabling multimodal agents to continually acquire useful information from complex, heterogeneous multimodal data remains a significant challenge as they move toward long-horizon tasks and lifelong settings. Addressing this challenge requires effective memory mechanisms that can maintain continuity across sessions, adapt to changing users and environments, and refine memory-management policies through accumulated experience. We introduce a two-axis analytical framework for multimodal agent memory structured around two key questions: how multimodal information is formed and represented (Axis I, Formation and Representation), and how its management adapts with accumulated experience (Axis II, Memory Management). Axis I, Formation and Representation, characterizes what information is retained and how it is encoded (e.g., modality-specific embeddings, textual and structured records, latent and parametric representations) to support subsequent reasoning and action. Axis II, Memory Management, distinguishes three tiers: T1 Static Memory reuses fixed memory; T2 Dynamic Memory updates memory through a stable policy; and T3 Self-Evolving Memory updates memory through an evolving policy. Based on this framework, we synthesize recurring design patterns and derive principles for balancing source fidelity with abstraction, maintaining temporal validity and provenance, grounding memory use in recoverable evidence, and evolving memory policies over time. Furthermore, we discuss the challenges and potential future directions for the memory mechanism of multimodal agents.

papers.title: Beyond Corrected Actions: Training LLM Agents on Textual Critiques
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for multi-turn agentic tasks that require interactions with users and environments over extended sequences of actions. A common approach to improving LLM agents is to use more capable expert models to provide training supervision, either by behavior cloning the expert's trajectories or by using the expert to correct the actions in trajectories generated by the weaker student model. However, expert LLMs can provide richer supervision than actions alone: they can directly generate textual critique that explain why specific actions are incorrect. We study whether training on such feedback benefits LLM agents and propose Critique-Augmented Agentic Fine-Tuning (CAFT), a framework that elicits textual expert feedback on student-generated trajectories. For each incorrect action, the expert yields both a corrected action and a textual critique explaining the student's mistake--which we then use as the training target for fine-tuning. Across four student models from the Nemotron 3 and Gemma 4 families on the agentic domains $τ^2$-Bench Airline+Retail and WebShop, adding critiques to action-level supervision improves performance by 8% on average over action-only distillation. Additionally, CAFT checkpoints can also provide a better warm start for reinforcement learning than expert-trajectory distillation. Our results demonstrate that textual critiques can strengthen supervision for multi-turn LLM agents.

papers.title: OS-Bench: Evaluating SWE Agents on Cross-OS Code Migration
papers.abstract: Language-model (LM) agents are increasingly evaluated on repository-level software engineering (SWE) benchmarks derived from GitHub issues and pull requests. Although these benchmarks cover a broad range of development tasks, they provide limited insight into a common yet technically distinct challenge: migrating an existing implementation from one operating system (OS) to another while preserving behavior on both. We introduce OS-Bench, an executable benchmark for cross-OS code migration between Linux and Windows. Motivated by case studies showing that cross-platform features are frequently implemented on one OS before support is added for another, OS-Bench identifies migration opportunities by comparing execution coverage collected from the same repository on both systems. Platform-specific regions are then verified, organized into five migration scenarios, and transformed into repository-level tasks with target-platform tests and source-platform regression tests. The resulting benchmark contains 140 validated tasks from 111 repositories across C, C++, C#, Go, and Rust, comprising 91 Windows-to-Linux and 49 Linux-to-Windows migrations. We evaluate six models with SWE-agent, Claude Code, OpenHands, and Win-agent. The best configurations achieve only 26.4% success on Linux-target tasks and 20.4% on Windows-target tasks while preserving correctness across both systems. These results indicate that cross-OS migration is a challenging and underexplored capability, and OS-Bench is a testbed for improving platform-aware SWE agents.

papers.title: The Impact of Detector Architecture, Model Scale, and Scene Density on Multi-Pedestrian Tracking
papers.abstract: Pedestrian tracking in video is important for applications such as surveillance and scene analysis, but it becomes more challenging in crowded scenarios with frequent occlusions and rapid motion. This paper analyzes how detector architecture, model scale, scene density, and inference regime affect the tracking of multiple pedestrians. We compare the YOLO11, RT-DETR, and YOLO26 detector families with the ByteTrack and BoT-SORT trackers on sequences from the MOT17, MOT20, and SOMPT22 benchmarks. For YOLO26, we also compare traditional overlap filtering via Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS) with end-to-end inference. The RT-DETR family achieved the highest mean scores on the HOTA tracking quality metric across all three benchmarks with both trackers, with a more pronounced advantage on MOT20, albeit at a higher computational cost. On MOT17 and SOMPT22, YOLO26 variants, especially YOLO26-L with NMS, offered favorable combinations of quality and speed compared with RT-DETR. In the YOLO26 inference comparison, the end-to-end mode did not yield consistent tracking gains over the NMS-based regime. Taken together, these results provide a practical guide for selecting detectors and trackers for this task based on application priorities.

papers.title: Odd-to-Even-Layer Switch of Spontaneous Excitonic State in $\rm{TiSe_{2}}$ Thin Films
papers.abstract: $\rm{TiSe_{2}}$ is a candidate of high temperature excitonic condensates with spontaneous exciton formation in addition to its charge density wave (CDW). However, direct observation and manipulation of this electron-hole paring state formation is still lacking. Here, using varying-temperature angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (VT-ARPES), we observe a distinct odd-to-even-layer switch of spontaneous exciton state formation with the evident correlated band structure in $\rm{TiSe_{2}}$ thin films. While the odd-layer $\rm{TiSe_{2}}$ films show a sharp band structure in single-particle picture superimposed by CDW renormalization, in the even-layer $\rm{TiSe_{2}}$ films, the full-filling valence band (VB) opens a distinct notch at the top, and the conductive band (CB) shows a significant extra signal extending above Fermi level with spectra broadening. These features indicate that the extra holes (notched VB) and electrons (broadening CB above Fermi level) form spontaneous excitons in even-layer $\rm{TiSe_{2}}$. Based on a correlated electron-hole model extracted from the tight-binding description, we reproduce the characterized band structures with spontaneous exciton formation, where the interlayer inter-band coupling in $\rm{TiSe_{2}}$ plays a key role, which leads to an odd-to-even-layer switch of the excitonic state formation. Our results provide direct evidences of the spontaneous exciton formation, promising an excitonic condensate as versatile platform for realizing Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) and investigating novel correlated phenomena.

papers.title: Analytically Optimal Sample Allocations for Nested Multivariate Multifidelity Control Variate Estimators
papers.abstract: Monte Carlo estimation, an essential tool for quantifying uncertainty in complex scientific and engineering applications, often has unacceptably large errors when computing resources are limited and each sample requires evaluating an expensive high-fidelity model. Multifidelity control variate methods seek to increase the accuracy of Monte Carlo estimation by combining a limited number of expensive high-fidelity samples with a larger number of cheaper lower-fidelity samples. Many different multifidelity estimators have been proposed, including multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC), multifidelity Monte Carlo (MFMC), approximate control variates (ACVs), and multilevel best linear unbiased estimators (MLBLUEs). An important design choice in multifidelity estimation is the allocation of a limited computational budget among the available models to minimize estimator error. The state of the art in solving this budget allocation problem relies on numerical optimization; to date, closed form solutions have only been derived for estimator forms known to be suboptimal. In this work, we provide closed form expressions for optimal fractional sample allocations for a large class of nested multifidelity control variate estimators, in which higher-fidelity models are evaluated on a subset of the inputs that lower-fidelity models are evaluated on. Our analysis is based on reformulating nested MLBLUEs as an extended version of the MFMC estimator, and is applicable to general multivariate Monte Carlo estimation. We additionally propose a new approach for integer-valued budget allocation based on a greedy strategy used in combinatorial optimization, as well as a method for robust approximation of control variate coefficients from limited pilot samples. Two numerical examples illustrate our theoretical results and demonstrate the increased accuracy of our extended MFMC formulation relative to existing estimators.

papers.title: Policy-Verified Self-Training: Learning Agent Compliance from Verifiable Policy Rewards
papers.abstract: Runtime policy verifiers can prevent agents from executing disallowed actions, but their decisions are typically used only for enforcement and discarded afterward. We ask whether these decisions can instead become verifiable policy rewards for training the agents they guard. We introduce Policy-Verified Self-Training (PVST), a post-training paradigm in which an agent generates its own interaction trajectories and an executable policy verifier, here a deterministic gate compiled from a written policy, evaluates whether each action complies. Compliant trajectories are reinforced, and violations become negatives for preference optimization; beyond the gate and the benchmark's task-success signal, PVST needs no stronger teacher model, no human preference labels and no attack-specific supervision, although rollouts are collected in the benchmark's attacked environment. On held-out AgentDojo tasks under prompt injection, policy-verified preference training of Qwen3-8B reduces violating trajectories from 37.2% to 10.3 $\pm$ 0.9% (three seeds) and successful attacks from 12.4% to 0.5% at equal or higher pooled task utility, although utility falls on travel, compared with 22.0% when negatives are selected by an attack oracle and 31.9 $\pm$ 0.9% with negatives that contain no violation. The learned behavior holds under an attack template never used in training (37.7% to 11.0%) and on a suite excluded from training (34.8% to 16.7%), and the retained verifier's intervention rate falls from 39.2% to 8.8% (seed 0). Our analysis identifies two conditions under which the verdict is most informative: success must not already imply compliance, and guarded actions must appear in both permitted and forbidden contexts.

papers.title: Evaluating Compressed Memory: Dependence, Utility, and Content Benefit
papers.abstract: Does a language model answer better because its compressed memory contains useful document information? Replacing memory vectors with zeros can lower a trained model's score without showing that it outperforms a model trained without memory.
