These advances make fully dynamical stellar fields practical for Bayesian and simulation-based inference.

papers.title: BANGLAPLAN: A Benchmark for Constraint-Based Planning and Decision-Making in Bangla
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly help users arrange appointments, plan journeys, and allocate limited resources. These tasks require models to satisfy constraints on time, cost, capacity, and order, or determine that no feasible solution exists. Bangla is the world's seventh most widely spoken language, and existing benchmarks cover many language and reasoning tasks. However, benchmarks for evaluating planning and decision-making in Bangla under explicit constraints remain lacking. We introduce BANGLAPLAN, a benchmark of 1,000 problems across ten task families grounded in everyday life and institutions in Bangladesh. It includes feasible and infeasible problems in four language registers: everyday, formal, colloquial, and Bangla--English mixed. Answers cover eight structured types, including schedules, routes, allocations, and ordered steps, in a common JSON format. We construct the benchmark through language-model-assisted drafting and independent human validation. We evaluate 11 open-weight and proprietary model configurations using exact match, separately reporting feasible-case accuracy, infeasibility detection, and format errors. We find a large performance gap: GPT-6.1 Sol achieves 98.7% accuracy and Qwen3.5-27B with thinking reaches 80.3%, while direct-answer configurations score at most 30.9%. Seven of eleven configurations perform below the always-``infeasible'' baseline. Our findings also suggest that harder problems primarily reduce plan-construction accuracy, while infeasibility detection remains more robust. BANGLAPLAN provides a reproducible basis for evaluating planning and decision-making in Bangla. BANGLAPLAN is available at: https://github.com/mrayhanulmasud/banglaplan.

papers.title: RouteWeaver: Weaving Mode Selection and Execution into Unified LLM Routing
papers.abstract: LLM routing dynamically selects and coordinates heterogeneous language models across diverse tasks. However, existing approaches are largely built around a predefined execution paradigm, such as single-round, multi-round, or agentic routing, which fixes how model calls are organized and limits adaptation to different query needs. We propose RouteWeaver, a unified routing framework that integrates these routing modes within a single LLM policy, jointly learning which mode to use and how to select models within that mode. To jointly optimize mode selection and within-mode execution, we develop COMET-GRPO (COordinated Mode-Execution Training), which decouples the trajectory-level advantage into separate signals for mode selection and within-mode execution, enabling more targeted credit assignment to each decision level. We further introduce progressive exploration, which gradually shifts training from externally assigned modes to autonomous selection, so that the router first learns how to execute each mode before deciding when to use it. We evaluate RouteWeaver across mathematics, coding, knowledge, logical reasoning, and factual recall. RouteWeaver achieves an average accuracy of 61.4%, an 11.03% relative improvement over the strongest baseline, and outperforms all compared baselines in each of the five domains. Ablations show that both COMET-GRPO and progressive exploration are important for adaptive routing; without progressive exploration, the routing policy collapses entirely to single-round execution.

papers.title: Graph Additive Models disentangling feature, topology, and interactions
papers.abstract: Graph Neural Additive Networks (GNANs) have emerged as effective, interpretable-by-design architectures for graph learning. They achieve transparency by combining per-feature shape functions with simple distance-based reweighting. However, GNANs have three limitations. First, node-wise relevance scores aggregate information from all graph nodes, allowing irrelevant nodes to inherit spurious relevance from relevant ones. Second, topology is represented only through shortest-path distances, so structurally distinct graphs may share identical distance profiles. Third, feature and distance information are combined multiplicatively, entangling feature, distance, and interaction effects in a single rescalable term. We introduce AMIGA, which represents topology through a vocabulary of mined motifs and decomposes each node contribution into three additive channels: feature, structure, and feature-structure interaction. The channels are centered around a graph-balanced training baseline, making the decomposition well-defined and unique under the chosen reference distribution. Across ten graph classification and regression benchmarks, AMIGA outperforms GNAN on most datasets and narrows the gap with standard black-box GNNs. Because each channel is centered and assigned to a single node, AMIGA produces node-local explanations that reconstruct the model output exactly and support interpretation at multiple levels of granularity.

papers.title: Revisiting Non-Adaptive Set Membership Schemes: Removing the Logarithmic Factor
papers.abstract: We study non-adaptive bit-probe schemes for static set membership. Each query reads a fixed number of bits and answers by strict majority. We revisit the random bipartite-graph construction of Garg and Radhakrishnan [STACS, 2017]. The main observation is that a slightly stronger expansion property already bounds the number of exceptional elements. This makes a separate probabilistic estimate for exceptional elements unnecessary. A detailed union-bound calculation then gives, for every fixed $t\ge5$, a logarithm-free existence bound of $O_t(m^{1/c}n^{1-1/c})$, where $c=\lfloor(t-1)/2\rfloor$. For odd $t$, this removes the logarithmic factor from the general upper bound of Garg and Radhakrishnan [STACS, 2017].

papers.title: The Weil-Petersson diameter of moduli space for large genus
papers.abstract: We determine the large-genus order of the Weil-Petersson diameter of $\mathcal{M}_{g,n}$ for each fixed number of punctures: namely, $\mathrm{diam}(\mathcal{M}_{g,n})\asymp\sqrt g\log g$. The main new ingredient is an integrated Ricci estimate for geodesics that minimize in moduli space and have thick endpoints, with no systole bound along their interiors.

papers.title: SceneAE: Scene Generation and Reconstruction in Queryable 3D-Anchored Latent Space
papers.abstract: Recent video world models have increasingly adopted 3D memory mechanisms to integrate historical observations into a lightweight and persistent scene representation. This naturally raises a complementary question: if 3D representations can serve as an effective mechanism for memorizing observed scenes, can they also be directly used as the latent space for reconstructing and generating scenes? Motivated by this idea, we represent a scene as a compact and unstructured 3D-anchored latent space (\textbf{SceneAE}). Each latent combines an explicit 3D position with an implicit content feature and is spatially grounded to describe its local scene region, forming a sparse latent point cloud. Unlike conventional video-VAE latents that describe how a scene appears from particular viewpoints, our representation directly describes the scene itself, making it naturally applicable to both reconstruction and generation. For reconstruction, once the scene has been generated, our persistent 3D representation can be projected and decoded into RGB-D observations by different target cameras, without the need to regenerate a video for each new camera trajectory. For generation, we leverage the geometry-content separation to first generate camera-controlled 3D geometry and then synthesize content conditioned on it, reducing camera-appearance entanglement and improving camera controllability. Experiments show that this 3D latent achieves superior generation quality, computational cost, and camera controllability.

papers.title: Beyond State Capacity: Why Retrieval Breaks in Mamba
papers.abstract: Mamba models underperform Transformers on in-context retrieval. This gap is usually attributed to Mamba's fixed-size recurrent state, which loses information as the context grows. We challenge this assumption by focusing on query-first retrieval, a setup in which the query precedes the context and state capacity should not be the binding constraint. We show that even in this setting Mamba lags substantially behind Transformers, despite its selection mechanism, which was designed to distinguish relevant content from distractors. We then demonstrate that the Mamba selection gates have sufficient control over the state updates to influence the model output: intervening on specific gates alone can swing accuracy between extremes. However, as gates are input-dependent, they require the incoming token's representation to encode its relevance to the query. We therefore probe token representations across layers, and find that the relevance signal emerges only gradually with model depth, and that the gates begin to reflect it only several layers deeper. Crucially, we find that gates in retrieval-critical layers are not yet aligned with relevance. The selection mechanism is thus expressive enough to solve the task, but it commonly operates on a relevance signal that has not yet arrived. Mamba's retrieval bottleneck therefore extends beyond state capacity: even when capacity is sufficient, the delayed emergence of relevance information across depth often prevents successful retrieval.

papers.title: Dynamic 3-Coloring of Bipartite Graphs with Optimal Locality
papers.abstract: We give a dynamic graph algorithm which maintains a 3-coloring in bipartite graphs under edge insertions such that the coloring only changes within a radius of $O(\log n)$ around an inserted edge. In the context of locality theory in distributed graph algorithms, this gives an upper bound on the locality under the dynamic-LOCAL model. Our bound on the locality is tight, as the problem admits a matching $Ω(\log n)$ lower bound in the stronger online-LOCAL model, by a result of Chang et al. [PODC 2024]. Thus, our result closes the gap between dynamic and online locality of this problem.

papers.title: Decoherence as a Detector-Resolution Flow
papers.abstract: We consider the QED final-state radiation modeled by $γγ^\ast\toπ^+π^-+X$, including its finite-temperature generalization, as an open quantum system, and study the evolution of the pion-pair momentum density matrix as the detector resolution scale is varied. We derive an explicit relation between the Lindblad jump operator and the Wilson line associated with soft photon radiation. We find that real emission and virtual correction serve as two separate contributions to momentum decoherence, and together they give rise to the real--virtual cancellation at the density-matrix level. The external finite-temperature photon bath modifies the decoherence rate by a Bose factor consistent with the Feynman--Vernon influence-functional approach. We emphasize that our conclusions also apply to hard fermion production thanks to the universality of the soft radiation.

papers.title: New Model, Old Habits: Behavior Transfer under Model Swapping in Multi-Session LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Multi-session agents can switch between LLMs to balance performance and inference cost. Such switches require transferring a history for continuity, yet their effects on the recipient remain underexplored. Through controlled experiments with multi-session tasks, we uncover behavior transfer: recipients tend to adopt reasoning and action patterns from the models that generated their histories. This effect is most evident with raw-history transfer but is substantially reduced by summarization. Based on these findings, we propose Direction- and Authorship-aware Summarization of History (DASH) that preserves stronger-model behavior while minimizing weak-to-strong transfer via summarization. Experiments with repeated swaps show that DASH outperforms raw-history transfer and naive summarization baselines. These results suggest that effective multi-model orchestration requires considering not only which model to use, but also which behavioral patterns to carry forward.

papers.title: Room-Temperature Metallic 2D Ferromagnetism Stabilized by Quantum Metric
papers.abstract: The recent discovery of long-sought dice-lattice bands in layered electride YCl opens up unprecedented opportunities for studying correlated electrons in real dice lattice systems. While the weakly dispersive band at the Fermi level is partially filled and density-wave states are expected due to Fermi surface nesting based on conventional theories, the ARPES measurement nevertheless revealed a uniform flat band splitting of 0.5 eV, suggesting unusual ferromagnetism (FM) borne out of the metallic 2D dice lattice. In this Letter, we propose that the uniform metallic FM order is stabilized by the prominent quantum metric near topological band crossing points at K and K', which reconstructs the magnetic instability in the dice metal and tips the density-wave instability toward a uniform FM order. Importantly, our analysis based on random phase approximation (RPA) and Hartree-Fock theory predicts a remarkably high Curie temperature above room temperature for the 2D FM order. These findings establish the first example of a room-temperature 2D metallic magnet stabilized by quantum metric, which not only exemplifies the fundamental significance of quantum geometry in solids but also bears far-reaching applications in energy-efficient high-density magnetic memories.

papers.title: Uncertainty-Driven Self-Play for Robust Multi-Agent Driving Policies
papers.abstract: Learning robust driving policies that generalize beyond their training domain remains a central challenge in motion planning. We propose an uncertainty-driven self-play scheme, in which half of the agents are rewarded for increasing their neighbors' epistemic uncertainty, while the other half learn to drive safely as the exploring agents continuously seek out their weaknesses. Epistemic uncertainty indicates where the policy is least confident and serves as an automatic proxy for scenario difficulty. Exploring agents use this signal to seek out hard cases, generating a challenging curriculum without manual scenario design. The resulting policy outperforms standard self-play, achieving best-in-class zero-shot transfer to nuplan Val14 (99.12% vs. 97.97%) and Argoverse 2 (82.39% vs. 78.03%) without fine-tuning, while also improving performance over standard self-play on Waymo. Our diversity-driven approach achieves 85% higher LSTM hidden-state coverage than the baseline, indicating a much richer set of behaviors. Further analysis shows that epistemic uncertainty serves as a calibrated difficulty detector, with highest-uncertain agents exhibiting 14.8 times the combined failure rate across collision, off-road, and DNF, of lowest-uncertain agents, enabling automatic prioritization of challenging scenarios without ground-truth labels.

papers.title: Capacity Bounds for Optical Interference Channels Subject to Average Power Constraints
papers.abstract: Accurate information-theoretic analysis of multiuser wavelength-division multiplexed (WDM) optical links is complicated by Kerr nonlinearity and chromatic dispersion. Existing capacity bounds for first-order regular perturbative (RP) channel models have relied on per-symbol peak power constraints to simplify the underlying extremal analysis. In this paper, we replace these peak constraints with the more practically relevant average input power constraints and study the resulting RP WDM interference channel. Unlike the peak-constrained formulation, an exact finite signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) analysis under average power leads in general to a nonconvex, high-dimensional optimization problem with no closed-form solution. We show that the problem admits a tractable characterization in the high-SNR regime. Using a genie-aided argument, we derive closed-form single-user high-SNR capacity bounds for the RP interference channel and identify constant-amplitude interferer signaling as extremal. Furthermore, under an empirically validated non-negativity condition on the dominant RP kernels and within a truncated first-order RP model, we establish a finite-SNR extremality result, yielding a single-user capacity characterization within the RP model under average power constraints. Building on these single-user corner points, we construct an all-helpsone achievable region via time sharing, which strictly improves upon treating nonlinear interference as noise. Numerical results and split-step Fourier simulations of the nonlinear Schrodinger equation channel confirm that the qualitative conclusions persist over practical launch powers. The results provide new insight into extremal signaling and multiuser trade-offs for nonlinear WDM systems within the RP approximation.

papers.title: Soloist: A Generative Model for Blind Voice Separation in the Wild
papers.abstract: Real-world voice separation must recover individual voices from overlapping speech, environmental noise, and music, yet isolated source recordings are rarely available for supervision. We introduce Soloist, a generative model for blind voice separation that autoregressively generates individual voice streams as audio-codec sequences conditioned on the mixture, without requiring a target-speaker query or a predefined voice count. We propose a two-stage training paradigm to learn from synthetic mixtures and adapt to real recordings. The first stage combines supervised separation on synthetic mixtures with isolated source targets and an auxiliary task that predicts speaker timelines from real recordings, learning who speaks when from natural acoustics. The second stage applies reinforcement learning to real recordings, with rewards supplied by a model judge that compares candidate separations based on voice purity and content preservation without isolated source targets. Across diverse scenarios, Soloist recovers clean speech from multi-speaker overlap and noisy recordings, and extracts singing vocals from music accompaniment while maintaining relatively high pitch accuracy and intelligibility. On real-world recordings with unknown voice counts, Soloist also separates voices well. Finally, we integrate Soloist into a full-duplex conversation processing pipeline that assembles separated outputs into continuous speaker tracks, demonstrating its practical utility in real conversations.

papers.title: No Way To Steal My Face: Proactive Defense Against Identity-Preserving Personalized Generation
papers.abstract: Recent advances in diffusion models have enabled high-fidelity, identity-preserving image generation for personalized applications such as digital avatars and virtual try-on systems. However, their reliance on sensitive facial reference images raises growing privacy concerns. Existing defense mechanisms are primarily designed for training-based personalization and struggle to generalize to emerging training-free approaches, due to fundamental differences in their identity integration paradigms. To bridge this gap, we propose IDGuardian-the first generalizable and model-agnostic identity protection framework capable of defending against both training-based and training-free personalization methods. IDGuardian abstracts the personalization process into two critical stages: identity extraction and identity injection. It then introduces crafted adversarial perturbations to simultaneously disrupt both stages. Specifically, it degrades the identity features extracted by external encoders and establishes an adversarial conceptual bridge that misdirects the generative trajectory away from the target identity. Extensive experiments show that IDGuardian effectively protects identity across various personalization pipelines and model architectures, while remaining robust to post-processing, adaptive attacks, and cross-dataset generalization. Our code is available at https://github.com/OpenAscent-L/IDGuardian.git.

papers.title: Evidence for Suppressed Non-thermal Broadening in a Flare Ribbon from Stereoscopic Observations
papers.abstract: Flare ribbons mark the footpoints of newly reconnected magnetic loops and are commonly associated with strong plasma flows and enhanced non-thermal broadening of transition-region lines due to impulsive energy deposition. However, the mechanisms governing energy transport into flare ribbons remain uncertain, particularly under different magnetic field configurations. We investigate the energy deposition process at a flare ribbon near a sunspot by determining the physical nature of its small-scale downflows. We study small-scale downflows in a remote ribbon during the M7.7-class event on 30 September 2024, using coordinated observations from SDO, IRIS, and Solar Orbiter. We use stereoscopic imaging from Solar Orbiter and IRIS to detect plane-of-sky motions on small scales (200 km). We conduct spectroscopic analysis of IRIS Si IV profiles, complemented by C II and Mg II diagnostics. Apparent downflow speeds measured from Solar Orbiter imaging (limb view) are 85-130 km/s, while IRIS images (disk view) reveal plane-of-sky speeds of 70-85 km/s. In contrast, IRIS Si IV profiles at the brightest ribbon pixels are well approximated by a single Gaussian, with minimal Doppler shifts and unexpectedly small non-thermal widths (10 km/s). Peak Si IV emission also coincides with a deeper Mg II central reversal, while electron densities are one to two orders of magnitude higher than typical quiet-Sun values. The absence of significant line-of-sight velocities and non-thermal broadening differs from typical flare-ribbon behavior. Our results are consistent with a scenario in which plasma motions are guided by highly inclined (nearly horizontal) magnetic fields in chromospheric canopy and are not accompanied by strong turbulence or wave motions. This study suggests that flare ribbons can exhibit a wide diversity of lower-atmospheric responses and emphasizes the critical role of magnetic field geometry.

papers.title: Learning Individual Scientific Taste with Privileged Hindsight Distillation
papers.abstract: Scientific taste shapes which research directions researchers pursue, and it varies across individuals. Existing work evaluates research directions along multiple evaluation criteria or models scientific taste using community feedback signals such as citations and reviews, but neither directly captures how individuals translate assessments under the same criteria into different preferences. We model scientific taste as a researcher-specific mapping from criterion-level assessments in a shared, evidence-grounded evaluation space with proposal-visible evidence, to relative preferences. A population-level mapping learned from retrospective supervision provides a cold start when individual feedback is scarce. We introduce Privileged Hindsight Distillation (PHD), which uses later-emerging scientific evidence during training to improve proposal-time criterion assessment and the population mapping, while exposing only proposal-visible information at inference. We evaluate our approach primarily in quantum research, where structured public reviews are largely unavailable, and use pairwise proposal comparison as a direct interface for observing individual taste. With only 15 comparisons per researcher, our method captures sharply different tastes, including opposing preferences over the same research-direction pairs when they trade off across evaluation criteria. In an interactive study, personalized rankings also surface proposals associated with greater subsequent user engagement, connecting learned taste to downstream research exploration.

papers.title: Which Text Matters: Handling Model Uncertainty in Text-as-Data Regressions, with an Application to Central Bank Communication
papers.abstract: Social scientists routinely convert text into covariates like topic shares, ideal points or sentiment scores, and insert them into statistical models of interest. This two-step design is convenient, but it is rarely guided by theory: little tells the analyst which text-based covariates to construct or include. Each approach embodies contestable measurement choices, and competing operationalizations of the same construct can support different conclusions, so a single research question gives rise to a menu of competing regression models. Which text constructed covariates belong in a model, and in what functional form, is thus a problem of model uncertainty. We propose spike-and-slab generalized additive models (SSGAMs), which jointly select covariates and determine whether their effects are linear or nonlinear. We illustrate the approach with the communication of a powerful unelected institution, asking which of 45 competing text indicators from 224 monthly European Central Bank press conferences, spanning late 2002 to mid-2025, track professional inflation expectations. A sparse set is selected; widely used alternatives, and every tested nonlinear effect, carry no incremental information.

papers.title: Articulation Upper Bounds for Language Models
papers.abstract: Language captures only a subset of the perceptions, intuitions and intents that form meaning between speakers. What, then, are the limits of language? We take steps towards measuring this in LLMs as follows: for a set of concepts, we measure how well each concept can be transmitted between two LLMs as their capabilities scale. This requires novel measurement tools: (1) optimal messages: we introduce a prompt optimization algorithm that beats existing algorithms by up to 14% on benchmarks and accurately estimates prompt upper bounds. (2) A transmission measure: the sender is asked to label text; the receiver then tries to recover the sender's prompt, and recovery is measured; we find this correlates strongly with human label error. With these measures, we use observational scaling laws to study how transmissibility of a concept, conveyed with optimal messages, increases as transmitter and receiver capacity grows: does it asymptote below or above a threshold? Measuring 1.2k concepts in eight domains, we find concepts that (a) can be fully articulated; these concepts usually depend on local patterns, e.g. "joke ends with surprise"; (b) might be articulated by future, stronger models; these rely on whole-text structural patterns, e.g. "story's worldbuilding coherence"; (c) concepts that face articulability limits; these concepts' meaning, we find, is tied to identity and social-group awareness, e.g. "comic voice". Interesting, these same concepts are not all challenging for humans: humans have moderate-to-high levels of agreement in 76% of concepts that LLMs struggle with; articulation limits, we find, are executor relative. Finally, we characterize the nature of improvement in each case: while recoverable concepts can be articulated through definitions and explanations, irrecoverable concepts cannot be transmitted, even with examples, and might require novel learning mechanisms.

papers.title: ONCship: A Large-Scale Underwater Acoustic Corpus for Ship Recognition
papers.abstract: Recent advances in deep learning have significantly improved underwater acoustic vessel recognition. However, existing publicly available datasets are typically limited in scale, hindering large-scale representation learning and downstream task evaluation. To address this limitation, we introduce ONCship, a large-scale underwater acoustic dataset comprising 4521 hours of curated recordings from Ocean Networks Canada (ONC) hydrophones and Automatic Identification System (AIS) data. We evaluate the proposed dataset across three tasks: self-supervised representation learning, vessel-type classification, and MMSI-Level Vessel Classification. Experiments on DeepShip and ShipsEar demonstrate the effectiveness of ONCship for acoustic representation learning, with joint pre-training on ONCship and AudioSet achieving a classification accuracy of 62.45% on DeepShip through linear probing. Furthermore, incorporating ONCship as auxiliary training data improves downstream vessel-type classification performance. Beyond conventional vessel-type classification, we further investigate MMSI-Level Vessel Classification, treating each vessel as a distinct identity. Experimental results show that models fine-tuned with different loss functions achieve Top-1 accuracies exceeding 53% and Top-5 accuracies approaching 69%, demonstrating the feasibility of distinguishing individual vessels through MMSI-Level Vessel Classification. Overall, ONCship provides a valuable resource for underwater acoustic representation learning and vessel recognition, while its rich vessel-level metadata enables further exploration of MMSI-Level Vessel Classification.

papers.title: Recognizing Dialogue Ambiguity via Candidate Set Visual Grounding
papers.abstract: Interpreting an ambiguous utterance in real-world interactions often requires context beyond a single utterance. When the utterance refers to objects in a visual scene, it is necessary to maintain and update the set of plausible referents as context accumulates, without assuming that the available information identifies a unique object. However, prior work on interactive visual grounding, which localizes objects referred to by linguistic expressions, has focused on identifying a unique object once sufficient dialogue context becomes available. To address this gap, we propose Candidate Set Visual Grounding (CSVG), a task for estimating the set of objects consistent with the given dialogue context. We further introduce CandVG, a benchmark that evaluates how the candidate set changes across dialogue turns. Our evaluation of vision-language models shows that stronger visual grounding capability does not necessarily yield better CSVG performance. In particular, models have difficulty predicting the complete candidate set, owing to challenges in candidate generation and premature commitment to a small set of candidates in early turns. Nevertheless, we find that this limitation can be partially mitigated in the evaluated large-scale models using instructions designed for CSVG.

papers.title: Graphs with Bounded Push-Pop Walk Orderings
papers.abstract: Consider a directed graph G and the (generally infinite) set Walks(G) of the walks in that graph. We are interested in ordering Walks(G) as w1, w2,... in a way that ensures that each walk is obtained from the previous one by a bounded number of elementary operations, namely, push operations (which add a new edge at either end of the walk) and pop operations (which remove the first or last edge of the walk). Our goal is to optimize the aforementioned bound, when it exists, in particular when imposing the additional requirement that walks must be ordered in increasing order of length. To this end, we introduce a condition on graphs inspired by earlier work, called inner-connectedness, which is testable in linear time; we show that inner-connected graphs are precisely those which admit bounded walk orderings. Focusing on such graphs, we then introduce and study the pp-rank and the pp-increasing-rank. Namely, the pp-rank of a graph is the best possible bound on the number of push-pop operations in a bounded walk ordering for that graph; and the pp-increasing-rank is the same where we further impose that shorter walks appear before longer walks in the ordering. We show that the pp-rank of inner-connected graphs is in fact always bounded by 3. The pp-increasing-rank of inner-connected graphs is also always finite, but it can be up to linear in the input graph. More precisely, we show that the pp-increasing-rank is related to a new parameter we introduce, the peripherality of graphs. In particular, for cyclic graphs, peripherality is related to the pp-increasing-rank up to multiplicative and additive constants. We last study how to compute these parameters, and show that while peripherality can be computed in polynomial time, the pp-increasing-rank itself is generally NP-hard to compute.

papers.title: TimeRSI: Towards Self-Improved Agentic Deployment for Time-Series Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Time-series foundation models provide strong zero-shot forecast, but deployment for real-world applications still requires task-specific designs for model inputs and outputs. Direct inference can leave domain knowledge and recurring forecast errors unaddressed, while tailored pipelines require substantial human expertise and effort. We introduce TimeRSI, a self-improving agentic deployment system around frozen forecasting models. A coding agent translates task descriptions into executable pipeline changes. It tests each revision on historical forecasting windows and uses observed errors to guide subsequent revisions. During deployment, an adaptive selector chooses among the resulting pipelines using completed forecasts under similar conditions. Across 198 tasks on TIME and fev-bench, TimeRSI outperforms all submissions on six point and probabilistic forecasting metrics. Controlled comparisons support the value of feedback-guided revision over non-iterative pipeline search. Further experiments verify the generalization with different coding agents and forecasting models. Code is available at https://github.com/haoxin1998/TimeRSI.

papers.title: Generative World Simulation with DAO and JING
papers.abstract: We present a Generative World Simulation framework that couples persistent shared world state with continuous first-person audiovisual generation. The framework integrates DAO, a computable world engine, and JING, an Egocentric Interactive Experience Model, to support sustained interaction for humans and agents. DAO maintains the states of characters, objects, and spaces and their relationships, advancing the world according to interaction rules and world time while preserving the consequences of past actions. From this evolving state, DAO derives observer-specific conditions for JING, which combines these conditions with character, object, and scene references, observation history, and current actions to generate each observer's audiovisual experience. Users can explore environments, manipulate objects, and communicate with characters through viewpoint control and text instructions, with their actions shaping both the shared state and subsequent experiences. By connecting world-state evolution with experience generation in a continuous interaction loop, the framework offers an approach to building interactive worlds that retain their history, evolve through action, and persist beyond any individual observer.

papers.title: Role of Gd 5d-Au 5d hybridization for the magnetic properties of Au-Al-Gd quasicrystal approximants
papers.abstract: We have studied the electronic states of magnetic Au-Al-Gd quasicrystal approximants, which exhibit different magnetic ground states at low temperatures, by orbital-selective soft and hard x-ray electron spectroscopies in the paramagnetic phase. Our results reveal that the valence electronic states vary among the Au-Al-Gd approximants with different magnetic ground states, whereas the Gd 4f electrons are localized in all of them. In particular, we find that the Gd 5d states are hybridized with the Au 5d states around the Fermi level, providing information about a local pathway for the intersite exchange interaction between the localized Gd 4f electrons. This hybridization strength varies among these samples. Our findings bring an orbital-resolved microscopic picture to the magnetism of rare-earth-based quasicrystals and approximants.

papers.title: Mitigating Video Hallucinations via Attention-Guided Representation Perturbation
papers.abstract: Video large language models (Video LLMs) often generate responses unsupported by the input video. Contrastive decoding (CD) can mitigate these hallucinations, but its effectiveness depends on how the negative branch weakens visual evidence. Existing methods rely on predefined perturbations or masking guided by question reconstruction, offering limited control over the model's visual reliance during answer generation. We introduce Attention-guided Representation Perturbation for Contrastive Decoding (ARP-CD), a training-free framework for constructing contrastive negatives directly in representation space. ARP-CD uses the attention mass assigned to visual tokens at the answer-prediction position to guide bounded gradient updates of the language model's input visual hidden states. These updates reduce visual attention and produce a negative input, whose predictions are contrasted with those of the original branch throughout generation. Experiments across four Video LLMs and four benchmarks show that ARP-CD outperforms representative training-free baselines in most model--benchmark settings, reducing hallucinations while improving general video understanding. Further analyses show that attention-guided perturbation directions improve negative quality and that the resulting negatives provide effective contrastive references for correcting the original predictions.

papers.title: A Diagnostic Study of World-Space Human Recovery Under High Camera Dynamics
papers.abstract: Monocular world-space human recovery methods excel on current benchmarks, but these rarely include fast camera motion. We introduce the K-Pop stress test, broadcast dance videos that combine fast, large camera motion with dense multi-person choreography. Leading methods produce plausible per-frame meshes on these videos, yet their world-space trajectories drift far from the performers' stage positions. Through a systematic diagnosis, we show that the camera and human estimates each remain self-consistent, and that the drift appears when they are combined at mismatched scales. Each is recovered at its own scale, so a mismatch between the two can turn camera motion into human drift that grows with camera displacement and becomes severe in broadcast dance videos. We derive a closed-form correction that estimates this mismatch and applies one scale to all performers, removing the drift while keeping their relative positions in one shared world frame. It requires no retraining and works with existing backends. Combined with physical constraints, the correction yields stable world-space reconstruction for choreography modeling, scene editing, data generation, and virtual reshooting. Project page: https://chien90190.github.io/worldhmr-fastcam-website/

papers.title: Design and Analysis of Temporal Representations in Neural Networks
papers.abstract: The ability to represent temporal information is often hypothesized to underlie the efficiency and learning capabilities of biological neural networks. This motivates the development of spiking neural networks. However, it remains unclear how temporal information is actually represented in neural networks and how different forms of temporal representation affect performance and computational efficiency. We introduce the notion of the degree of temporal representation of a neural network, defined by whether its constituent functions (activation, learning, encoding, and decoding) explicitly manipulate time as a computational variable. This perspective yields a continuum ranging from non-temporal representations, where time does not explicitly appear as a computational variable in the network functions, to fully temporal representations, where computations explicitly operate on temporal variables. Using a fixed deep architecture, we compare different encoding, activation mechanisms and decoding with increasing temporal expressiveness: non-temporal weighted-sum activations used in usual artificial neural networks, non-temporal binary spiking activations used in spiking neural networks, and spike-time-based activations used in delay neural networks. Experiments on event-based datasets show that increasing the degree of temporal representation improves both performance and computational efficiency, allowing state-of-the-art performances on the Google Speech Commands dataset. We further analyze how temporal representations induce distinct forward and backward computational trajectories, leading to gradients that depend explicitly on the history of event times.

papers.title: What Happens to the Goal? Distinct Failures of Policy Alignment in Goal Misgeneralization
papers.abstract: Goal misgeneralization is a common failure mode in which an agent behaves competently out of distribution but pursues a proxy that coincided with the intended goal during training instead of the goal itself. However, we still have a weak understanding of what happens to the intended goal in misgeneralizing agents and what enables them to be recovered without retraining. We study this across eight visual navigation and manipulation tasks, including robot control. While tracing where goal information remains available internally, how strongly it influences the policy, and what role it plays in action selection, we uncover that the goal is lost at one of three different depths. This depth predicts which recovery works in each task. When the goal is followed, but outcompeted by the proxy, steering the existing policy redirects it to the goal's location, raising goal reach from 16.0% to 95.3%. When it is read, but not followed, steering fails, but a lightweight new downstream wiring recovers goal reach from 31.6% to 84.3%. When it is not read, none of the methods work, as the policy does not use the goal information. The same tracing also reveals what replaces the goal: functional target substitution, where behavior follows an alternative goal, a policy shortcut, where behavior follows a learned action strategy, or cue competition between intended and proxy goal cues. Knowing where the goal is lost tells us whether an agent can be repaired or has to be retrained. Goal misgeneralization should therefore be studied and evaluated inside the agent, not only from its behavior.

papers.title: RL Teaches VLMs Where to Attend but Not How to Perceive
papers.abstract: Although reinforcement learning (RL) effectively trains Vision-Language Model (VLM) agents, the mechanisms behind these capability gains are poorly understood. Across four diverse agent environments, we investigate whether the task-success gains from multi-turn RL are accompanied by improved grounded visual question answering about the environment. To assess this, we design environment-specific grounded VQA tasks that reveal improvements in grounded visual understanding. Representational probing shows that vision-encoder probe accuracy remains relatively stable, while LLM-layer probe accuracy improves. Attention analysis further reveals that LLM layers pay more attention to visual tokens during RL training. To test whether increased attention to visual tokens contributes to VQA gains, we introduce a lightweight plug-and-play intervention using a fixed attention bias. Without updating model parameters or computing gradients, this intervention partially restores VQA gains on the untrained model. These results reveal better utilization of visual information as a key mechanism behind the gains from RL.

papers.title: When the implementation matters more than the algorithm: NSGA-II and other multi-objective optimizers in engineering design tools
papers.abstract: Engineering design tools increasingly embed optimizers as ready-made components that users select by algorithm name, while operator settings and bound, integer and duplicate handling stay fixed inside each tool. This study tests whether the name predicts the result. A tool-agnostic harness exposes one deterministic black box, an emulator of a published 22-variable mixed-integer building-performance problem, to the native optimizers of three Grasshopper plug-ins, to canonical NSGA-II, SMS-EMOA and GDE3 from Python libraries, and to the model-based RBFMOpt. Eighteen configurations were run at 5,000 evaluations under three population allocations, with statistics fixed in advance. Four NSGA-II implementations differed by up to 5% in hypervolume, more than three canonical algorithms of different families differed from one another, and their response to population size differed by up to 10 percentage points; for two MOEA/D implementations, by 28. On ZDT test functions the same NSGA-II implementations differed up to 470-fold in IGD. An ablation in one open-source NSGA-II reproduced the behaviour of one tool from its documented settings but not the gaps of the other two, so documented parameters do not identify an implementation. Counting the budget in wall-clock time reversed the ranking of the model-based optimizer, and reporting the final population instead of the archive understated some configurations by up to a third; most differences fell below the surrogate's error. For optimizers embedded in design-support systems, the implementation is part of the method; a reporting checklist is derived: implementation and version, effective settings, budget in time and evaluations, and archive-based indicators.

papers.title: Controlling the latency in temporal coded spiking models for neuromorphic datasets
papers.abstract: Exploiting temporal information in datasets with high temporal dependencies (such as spoken keyword recognition) by spiking models is still an open problem. Promising frameworks include Time-To-First coding (TTFS) and the inclusion of synaptic delays into learning. In TTFS, neurons are forced to spike at most once, forcing the network to found its learning on the spiking times of neurons rather than their spiking rate. Some models use the TTFS framework to directly compute the spiking time of Integrate-and-Fire (IF) or Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neurons. However, most models built in the TTFS framework have not been tested against datasets containing temporal information. Little is known about the latency of these models on temporal datasets, where the latency is the time taken by the network to correctly classify a sample. In this work, we study the behaviour of Delay Neural Networks (DeNN) models, i.e. models that directly compute the spiking time of neurons by bypassing the membrane potential and thresholding mechanisms of spiking neurons. We show how to analytically control their latency, and empirically study the latency-accuracy tradeoff in a dynamic temporal dataset.

papers.title: Dynamical entropy and thermodynamics of causal diamonds
papers.abstract: We study the dynamical entropy of causal diamonds using Wald-Zoupas charges and fluxes on their null boundaries. For a chosen boundary symplectic potential, the boost charge defines an entropy made of an area term plus an expansion correction, which reduces to one quarter of the area at the edge on the diamond. In Einstein gravity, we find an exact balance law relating the entropy on any two cuts of the null boundary to a signed flux, so the entropy decreases only when this flux is non-negative. We obtain a linearised physical process first law without assuming a background Killing symmetry, both in the presence and absence of external matter; and extend it for semiclassical gravity based on the improved quantum null energy condition. We also examine causal diamonds in maximally symmetric spacetimes and in Einstein-scalar gravity.

papers.title: Exact Cut Complexity of Equal-Length Proportional Cake Cutting
papers.abstract: We study proportional cake cutting under an equal-length constraint, where each of $n$ agents must receive a bundle of length exactly $1/n$ that is worth at least $1/n$ to that agent. Our main result determines the exact worst-case number of cuts needed to guarantee such an allocation, namely $2n-2$ for every $n$. This improves on the previously known quadratic upper bound. The proof combines the constrained necklace-splitting theorem with a recursive assignment argument based on Hall's theorem. The same bound extends to the stronger requirement of envy-freeness when $n$ is a prime power, and an $O(n^{1.525})$ upper bound holds for arbitrary $n$. We then ask whether such allocations can be computed. We first show that no deterministic protocol in the Robertson--Webb model terminates after finitely many queries on every instance and always returns an exact equal-length proportional allocation, even for two agents with identical valuations. For every $\varepsilon>0$, however, $O(n^2/\varepsilon)$ queries suffice to produce an allocation in which every agent receives a bundle of length exactly $1/n$ and value at least $1/n-\varepsilon$, again using at most $2n-2$ cuts. Finally, we augment the Robertson--Webb model with two-knife queries. We show that recursive balanced halving attains the optimal bound of $2n-2$ cuts when $n$ is a power of two. For arbitrary $n$, we give a procedure using $O(n\log n)$ cuts.

papers.title: Object Pose from 2-D to 3-D Point and Line Correspondences
papers.abstract: In this paper we present a method for optimally estimating the rotation and translation between a camera and a 3-D object from point and/or line correspondences. First we devise an error function and second we show how to minimize this error function. The quadratic nature of this function is made possible by representing rotation and translation with a dual number quaternion. We provide a detailed account of the computational aspects of a trust-region optimization method. This method compares favourably with Newton's method which has extensively been used to solve the problem at hand, with Faugeras-Toscani linear method [6] for calibrating a camera, and with the Levenberg-Marquardt non-linear optimization method. Finally we present some experimental results which demonstrate the robustness of our method with respect to image noise and matching errors.

papers.title: MakSafe: A Spatiotemporal Semantic Framework for Formal Specification and Compliance Checking of Road Vehicle Safety Rules
papers.abstract: Scenario-based validation is essential for automated road vehicles but cannot cover the full variability of openworld traffic. We present MakSafe, a formal spatiotemporal framework for specifying and checking road vehicle safety rules through semantic zones, action-based forecasting, and trace-tree reasoning, avoiding uniform time discretization. We formalize the road network, vehicle states, and occupancy zones, then build executable rules for front-vehicle identification and timeto-collision (TTC) verification. The evaluation combines a tracedependent case study with a scalability benchmark over traffic density (N ), horizon (H), and branch factor (B). MakSafe yields branch-specific verdicts, deriving safe and unsafe outcomes from the same initial scene, and re-evaluates a scenario after a control update. A single rule check stays well below a millisecond across the reported sweep, and longer horizons slow the TTC check.

papers.title: Void-Free Through-Glass Vias for Multilayer Surface-Electrode Ion Traps
papers.abstract: Through-substrate interconnects are a key technology for scaling surface-electrode ion traps (SEITs) toward large electrode counts and complex architectures. Dielectric substrates such as fused silica offer superior RF performance compared to silicon, but the reliable fabrication of void-free through-glass vias (TGVs) remains challenging. In this work, we demonstrate a SEIT fabricated on a fused silica substrate incorporating TGVs. The via-holes are formed using Selective Laser-Induced Etching and subsequently metallized with gold by electroplating. A patent-pending geometry-assisted bottom-up plating approach enables void-free filling using constant-current electroplating without electrolyte additives or pulsed deposition schemes. Electrical characterization across multiple wafers confirms a TGV-level yield above 98.8 %, demonstrating the robustness and reproducibility of the developed TGV technology. The TGVs are combined with multilayer SEIT fabrication, enabling vertical signal routing to all electrodes while maintaining an unaffected trapping surface without wire bonds. To interface the trap with external control electronics, a glass interposer providing signal fan-out to a larger pitch is designed and fabricated. The trap chip and the interposer are integrated using thermocompression bonding, forming a compact chip-to-chip assembly. The presented technology demonstrates the first fully integrated multilayer SEIT on fused silica incorporating void-free TGVs.

papers.title: Gaussian approximation for the integrated intensity of counting processes: application to Hawkes processes
papers.abstract: In this paper, we establish quantitative central limit theorems for the integrated fluctuations of the intensity of a counting process. Building on the work of Coutin and using the Clark-Ocone formula, we first derive a general upper bound on the Wasserstein distance between a Gaussian random variable and the normalized integral of the centered intensity. We then apply this result to subcritical linear Hawkes processes. In this setting, we prove that the integrated fluctuations of the intensity converge in distribution to a centered Gaussian random variable, with a convergence rate governed by the tail behavior of the resolvent associated with the underlying Volterra equation.

papers.title: ProtModernBERT: Compute-Efficient Protein Language Modeling
papers.abstract: Large protein language models provide a powerful framework for learning sequence-function relationships and guiding experimental design. However, architectural improvements are underexplored, especially in low-compute regimes of relevance for resource-constrained research laboratories. We show that the training cost for encoder-only transformer architectures can be reduced by leveraging modern architectural refinements, offering an encouraging performance / compute-efficiency trade-off. We introduce ProtModernBERT, a modernized BERT-style model pre-trained on amino acid sequences, and compare it with ProtBert, Amplify, and ESM2 across a set of supervised structural tasks -encompassing secondary structure prediction, disorder prediction, and subcellular localization- and ProteinGym's zero-shot functional benchmark. We find that ProtModernBERT matches or closely tracks the performance of Amplify-120M and ProtBert with up to 80-90\% reduction in pre-training FLOPs, and narrows the gap to ESM2 when controlling for pre-training. Our analysis using a cluster-based validation protocol for hyperparameter selection and randomly initialized models disentangles the contributions of architecture and data, showing that modern components provide stronger inductive biases that are more consequential than parameter count in low-compute regimes.

papers.title: High-Frequency Transverse Waves in Chromospheric Fibrils Revealed by DKIST
papers.abstract: Chromospheric fibrils are ubiquitous dynamical structures that can support magnetohydrodynamic waves and may contribute to energy transport in the solar atmosphere. Using high-resolution observations from the Visible Broadband Imager (VBI) onboard the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope (DKIST), we investigate transverse oscillations of H$α$ fibrils. Our observations encompass both quiet-Sun and active regions. The results reveal that high-frequency transverse oscillations are highly prevalent in fibrils across different magnetic environments. The detected oscillations exhibit typical periods of 56 $\pm$ 49 s, displacement amplitudes of 37 $\pm$ 25 km, velocity amplitudes of 6 $\pm$ 4 km\,s$^{-1}$, and phase velocities of 21 $\pm$ 13 km\,s$^{-1}$. Under typical chromospheric conditions, the estimated wave energy flux ranges from 20 to 200 W\,m$^{-2}$. The characteristics of these transverse oscillations are consistent with those of Alfvénic kink-mode waves. Our results reveal the existence of the high-frequency, small-amplitude transverse waves in chromospheric fibrils and providing new constraints on their contribution to the chromospheric and coronal heating.

papers.title: Asymptotic stability and Rayleigh-Taylor instability of stratified states for the three-dimensional rotating primitive equations with gravity
papers.abstract: We study the 3D rotating primitive equations with gravity in a horizontally periodic channel, with viscous horizontal velocity and no density diffusion. For every Coriolis parameter, stably stratified equilibria are asymptotically stable. Small compatible \(H^4\) perturbations yield global classical solutions with uniform \(H^4\) bounds. The oscillatory density and velocity decay like \((1+t)^{-1}\); the density converges at the same rate to a stratified profile, its horizontal mean faster. For small data, the limit profile is the decreasing vertical rearrangement of the initial density, the unique potential-energy minimizer among rearrangements, independent of rotation, viscosity, and initial velocity. Kinetic plus available potential energy is dissipated exactly by viscosity and decays like \((1+t)^{-2}\), and each fluid particle settles where the limit density equals its own. These rates are optimal for every rotation rate. The linearized problem has real, slowly decaying normal modes, viscously overdamped high-vertical-wavenumber internal gravity waves, whose small solutions show the \(H^r\) density rates \((1+t)^{-(1-r/4)}\), \(0\le r<4\), pressure rate \((1+t)^{-1}\), and energy rate \((1+t)^{-2}\) cannot be improved uniformly for small data. Key difficulties are the loss of a horizontal derivative in the vertical velocity, the failure of \(H^1(\mathbb T^2)\subset L^\infty\), and rotation-induced coupling of divergent and vortical motion, controlled at top order by a positive power of the initial low-order energy. If the stratification is unstable somewhere, every horizontal mode is linearly unstable with real growth rates and the equilibrium is nonlinearly unstable; rotation strictly lowers each growth rate, with an explicit Taylor-number bound depending on the horizontal wavelength, but leaves their supremum unchanged.

papers.title: Does the Linguistic Register of Thinking Matter? Wenyan as a Compact Reasoning Register for Chinese LLMs
papers.abstract: Visible reasoning traces of Chinese reasoning-oriented LLMs are typically written in modern vernacular Chinese, which may be verbose under limited decoding budgets. We ask whether the linguistic register of reasoning can be used to improve efficiency. We propose Wenyan Thinking, which emits intermediate reasoning in Classical Chinese (wenyanwen) while retaining a short direct-answer output. Starting from modern-Chinese reasoning traces, we rewrite only the reasoning field into wenyan and fine-tune Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 on the rewritten supervision. To distinguish register shift from generic compression, we construct a compact modern-Chinese control using the same source data, teacher family, base model, and SFT recipe. Across budget-sensitive evaluations on MMLU-ProX-Lite-ZH, CEVAL, and AGIEval-CN, Wenyan Thinking substantially reduces reasoning length and missing-answer rates under constrained decoding. Compact rewriting explains much of the efficiency gain, while wenyan consistently outperforms the compact modern-Chinese control on the primary benchmark and remains competitive across the additional benchmarks. These results identify linguistic register as a practical design axis for efficient visible reasoning in Chinese LLMs.

papers.title: HyperLoop: Hyperspectral-Assisted Loop Closure Detection in 3D-SLAM for Planetary Exploration
papers.abstract: Autonomous navigation of planetary rovers is challenged by visually repetitive, featureless terrain. SLAM systems based on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) offer dense mapping but rely on RGB appearance descriptors that degrade under perceptual aliasing - a common failure mode in extraterrestrial environments where physically distinct locations appear visually identical. This paper presents HyperLoop, the first framework integrating hyperspectral imaging (HSI) into the loop closure module of a 3DGS-based SLAM system. Hyperspectral descriptors encode material-level spectral signatures complementing RGB features, providing robustness to illumination changes and visual repetitiveness. Two HSI descriptor families are introduced: Bag-of-Spectral-Words (BoSW), encoding spectral material distributions via TF-IDF weighted histograms, and PCA-K VLAD (PCAK-VLAD), capturing first-order residual statistics of PCA-compressed spectral signatures. Both are evaluated with SIFT-VLAD and NetVLAD RGB descriptors under Strict-AND and Weighted fusion strategies on a custom dataset from the Moon-Mars Outdoor Test Site (MMOTS) at DLR, comprising synchronized RGB-D and hyperspectral sequences across four planetary analog traverses (65.5 m total). A key finding is that the sensor's Red-NIR range (600-860 nm) provides limited discriminability for rock terrain: the best HSI fusion (SIFT-VLAD + BoSW, Strict-AND) achieves 5.04 cm ATE RMSE, within 1.8% of SIFT-VLAD alone (4.95 cm). The gain over NetVLAD (8.81 cm) is attributable to SIFT-VLAD, not HSI fusion. This motivates future adoption of SWIR sensors capturing diagnostic mineral absorption features absent from the 600-860 nm range for planetary SLAM missions.

papers.title: Discriminative Score Function: Turning Pretrained Models into Functional Generative Priors
papers.abstract: Discriminative models are trained with task-specific objectives such as classification, detection, or representation learning, yet their practical utility depends on generalizing beyond the training task to unseen samples from the same domain. This suggests that a discriminative model may retain an implicit trace of the data manifold beyond its task labels. We ask whether this trace can be exposed as a generative signal without task-specific guidance. We introduce the Discriminative Score Function (DSF), which extracts an image-space generative field from the loss-gradient geometry of a pretrained discriminative model. DSF provides a training-free update rule that moves images toward model-consistent visual regions without retraining or task-specific targets. We apply DSF to diverse pretrained discriminative models, including ResNet classifiers, DETR detectors, and DINOv2 ViT encoders. DSF generates unconditional images from noise and supports conditional guidance, editing, inpainting, and explanation through the same field. DSF-generated samples also provide effective zero-shot quantization calibration when real images or labels are unavailable, preserving feature geometry better than data-free calibration baselines. These results show that discriminative training leaves a generative functional signal for synthesis and calibration. Project page: https://junhoo.me/dsf.

papers.title: Resolving Structural Uncertainty in Stochastic Dynamical Systems via Ensemble-Based Bayesian Inference
papers.abstract: Recovering the interaction structure of complex stochastic dynamical systems from sparse time-series observations is an inherently ill-posed inverse problem. The posterior over network configurations is high-dimensional, highly degenerate, and shaped by the non-equilibrium nature of the available data. To address this, we propose a fully Bayesian, ensemble-based inference framework. Our approach grounds a continuous-time Stochastic Differential Equation (SDE) likelihood formulation---acting mathematically as an Onsager-Machlup quasi-potential for non-equilibrium paths---within a non-parametric Minimum Description Length (MDL) structural prior. This framework rigorously penalizes model complexity and avoids kinetic overfitting by forcing continuous parameters into a finite vocabulary of discrete categories. The joint posterior is optimized using a block-coordinate scheme combining sub-quadratic Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) topological sampling with deterministic Nelder-Mead parameter optimization. Using highly non-linear macroscopic population dynamics as a benchmark, we demonstrate that inference requires non-stationary transient data to resolve causal information. Furthermore, we prove that propagating structural uncertainty via ensemble-based posterior analysis produces significantly more robust and reliable predictions for downstream perturbation outcomes than traditional single-point (MAP) estimates. The framework is highly generalizable, capturing fundamental topological constraints even under severe generative model mismatches, offering a robust tool for uncertainty-aware inference in complex stochastic systems.

papers.title: Continuous and compact embeddings for a class of modular sequence spaces
papers.abstract: In this article we prove the existence of continuous and compact embeddings for a class of modular sequence spaces generated by Orlicz functions. The class under consideration contains sequence spaces of Orlicz-Sobolev type, including certain special cases that have played an important role in a number of applications regarding problems arising in non-equilibrium statistical mechanics, as well as Nakano's class of Lebesgue sequence spaces with variable exponents. In a few exceptional cases we provide necessary and sufficient conditions for such embeddings to hold, in many others only sufficient conditions and in that situation we clearly indicate why these are not necessary by means of additional criteria and specific examples. Our results are complementary to those already available in the literature. We illustrate them with several concrete examples.

papers.title: One-shot Human Video-Guided Adaptation for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have recently achieved remarkable progress by leveraging large-scale robot datasets and foundation models for general-purpose robot manipulation. However, their ability to rapidly adapt to novel manipulation tasks beyond the training distribution remains limited. Existing approaches often require task-specific robot demonstrations and additional training, which are labor- and compute-intensive, limiting the scalability of VLA adaptation to open-world scenarios. To reduce this dependence on target-task robot data, we propose CapPro, a framework that enables a VLA policy to adapt to previously unseen manipulation tasks using only a single human demonstration video. CapPro consists of two components. First, a phase-aware human video representation module constructs a compact video representation through learned visual token selection and learns task-relevant query representations under phase-caption supervision. Second, a video-conditioned adaptation module jointly incorporates the compact video and query-derived representations into the action-conditioning context of the pretrained VLA policy. % This design introduces task-specific guidance while largely preserving the original VLA action-generation backbone. In this way, the human demonstration provides task-specific execution guidance rather than an embodiment-aligned trajectory to imitate, without requiring target-task robot demonstrations or target-task fine-tuning. Experiments across source and unseen target tasks show that CapPro improves average performance across unseen target groups while maintaining comparable performance on the source tasks. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of human-video guidance for cross-task VLA adaptation.

papers.title: Generalized Odds for Ordinal Outcomes: A Causal Inference Framework Adjusting for Covariates
papers.abstract: Background: Generalized Odds (Gen Odds) provide summaries for ordinal outcomes without requiring the proportional odds assumption. However, conventional Gen Odds compares independently drawn treatment and control outcomes and targets a population-level contrast rather than an individual-level contrast. We developed an individual-level causal formulation of Gen Odds and examined its identification. Methods: We defined the Causal Gen Odds using the joint distribution of potential outcomes and identified it under conditional independence of the potential outcomes given baseline covariates. We developed a model-based estimator using nonproportional cumulative logistic regression and introduced an odds-ratio sensitivity parameter to assess departures from conditional independence. We evaluated the estimators through simulations and illustrated them using data from the ACCORD Study. Results: In simulations, the conditional-independence estimator was approximately unbiased with 95.5% confidence interval coverage under conditional independence, but bias and undercoverage increased with residual dependence. When the sensitivity-analysis estimator incorporated the data-generating dependence parameter, bias remained below 0.01 and coverage ranged from 93.7% to 96.1% across examined settings. In the ACCORD Study, the Causal Gen Odds for right-foot pre-tibial edema was 0.909 (95% CI: 0.880 to 0.940) under conditional independence and remained stable across the examined sensitivity range. Conclusions: The Causal Gen Odds provides an individual-level estimand that complements the conventional population-level Gen Odds. This framework enables estimation of this contrast while explicitly assessing its robustness to assumptions about dependence between potential outcomes.

papers.title: Finite Volume Methods
papers.abstract: This chapter focuses on finite volume methods. The finite volume method is a discretization method that is well suited for the numerical simulation of various types (for instance, elliptic, parabolic, or hyperbolic) of conservation laws; it has been extensively used in several engineering fields, such as fluid mechanics, heat and mass transfer, or petroleum engineering. Some of the important features of the finite volume method are similar to those of the finite element method: it may be used on arbitrary geometries, using structured or unstructured meshes, and it leads to robust schemes. The finite volume method is locally conservative because it is based on a ``balance'' approach: a local balance is written on each discretization cell that is often called ``control volume;'' by the divergence formula, an integral formulation of the fluxes over the boundary of the control volume is then obtained. The fluxes on the boundary are discretized with respect to the discrete unknowns.

papers.title: Global well-posedness of the energy-critical nonlinear Schrödinger equation on the three-dimensional torus with additive Lévy noise
papers.abstract: This paper establishes global well-posedness for the defocusing energy-critical nonlinear Schrödinger equation on the three-dimensional torus with a class of additive Lévy noises. For arbitrary deterministic initial data in the energy space, we construct probabilistically strong solutions that are pathwise unique in the critical solution class. Continuous dependence on initial data, convergence of finite-activity approximations, and a vanishing-noise limit hold on finite time intervals. When the effective noise is nonzero, quantitative bounds for mass exit times imply almost-sure unboundedness of the mass and exclude free scattering. The expected energy then admits a cubic lower bound in time. The analysis couples pathwise critical perturbation theory with energy estimates adapted to Poisson compensation and stopping-time arguments based on the exact mass balance.

papers.title: Crystallization of the undertile
papers.abstract: We classify all periodic tilings with a monotile known as $\mathbf{R1}$ and called here the undertile, which underlies several aperiodic monotiles such as the Taylor-Socolar one. The classification is done using deflation, through a study of fracture lines between zones where deflation can be performed. A full classification of fracture patterns is given, that also applies to non-periodic tilings with the undertile. This can be used to reprove non-periodicity of some existing monotiles based on the undertile.

papers.title: Severity-Aware Minimum Security Sets for Accelerated Preventive SCOPF Using Machine Learning
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a severity-aware machine learning framework for reducing the computational burden of preventive AC security-constrained optimal power flow (PSCOPF). The central idea is to identify a compact minimum security set (MSS) containing only the non-dominated contingencies and associated post-contingency constraints that materially influence the preventive operating point while satisfying a prescribed severity tolerance. An offline procedure combines AC security assessment, severity-based ranking, non-dominated screening, and iterative reduced PSCOPF. After each reduced PSCOPF solution, exhaustive security assessment over all credible contingencies identifies additional contingency--constraint pairs whose residual severity exceeds the specified threshold. Severity is characterized using the normalized number, accumulated magnitude, maximum magnitude, and average magnitude of post-contingency violations. The resulting operating-point-dependent MSSs are used as labels for a supervised multi-label learning model that predicts the security elements required to construct the reduced PSCOPF directly from the pre-contingency state. The proposed framework therefore focuses the optimization on the contingencies and constraints that affect preventive control decisions, reducing problem size and computation time while explicitly controlling residual post-contingency severity. Results on the IEEE 60-bus and 118-bus systems, the latter having an approximately seven-times-larger PSCOPF formulation, demonstrate substantial computational reductions with limited impact on the preventive operating solution.

papers.title: Quantum-enhanced Search for Galactic Dark Photons Using Cat-State Cavities
papers.abstract: We present a quantum-enhanced search for the Galactic dark-photon background (GDPB), a relativistic and anisotropic vector field that can be produced by dark-matter decay or annihilation in the Milky Way halo. We reinterpret an existing quantum-enhanced dark-photon dataset obtained with a superconducting circuit QED platform originally developed for wave-like dark-photon dark-matter searches, consisting of a high-$Q$ niobium cavity in the $\mathrm{TM}_{010}$ mode dispersively coupled to a transmon qubit. By preparing four-component cat states and performing repeated quantum non-demolition parity measurements, analyzed with a hidden Markov model, we extract photon-transition probabilities for multiple cat amplitudes and integration times. The coupling to the GDPB is governed by a polarization- and angle-dependent cavity overlap function, which predicts a distinctive diurnal modulation of the excitation rate for both longitudinal and transverse polarizations. From the absence of such modulation, we set 90\% confidence-level bounds on the kinetic-mixing parameter $ε$ for two benchmark production mechanisms (parametric and cascade decay) over the relativistic mass range $m_X \ll ω_c$.

papers.title: Quantum-enhanced phase interrogation of a fiber-optic strain sensor
papers.abstract: Fiber-optic sensors enable high-sensitivity measurements of various physical parameters. Here, we demonstrate a quantum-enhanced interrogation of an all-fiber-optic Fabry-Perot resonator, employing entangled two-photon interference to probe directly strain-induced optical phase shifts. The resonator is interrogated by a narrow-linewidth laser that is frequency-locked to its resonance mode, thereby exploiting the cavity's inherent sensitivity to variations in the fiber length. To access the phase fluctuations transferred to the interrogation field due to external perturbations on the sensor, we implement an in-fiber Mach-Zehnder interferometer readout. This configuration allows the sensor to operate both with classical coherent light and with entangled photon pairs generated via spontaneous parametric down-conversion. Harnessing two-photon entangled states corresponding to an N = 2 NOON state, we experimentally demonstrate a reduction of the measurement noise below the standard quantum limit. These results provide clear evidence of the quantum advantage in enhancing fiber-optic sensors under practical constraints on optical power.

papers.title: Coordi-pi: Coordination-Aware Dual-Hand Action Representation for Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong potential for general-purpose robotic manipulation, but extending them to bimanual dexterous manipulation introduces a high-dimensional and structured action space. Existing bimanual VLA policies commonly concatenate right- and left-side arm--hand actions at each control timestep, leaving cross-hand interactions implicit within a single action vector. We introduce Coordi-$π$, a structured action representation for bimanual dexterous manipulation. Coordi-$π$ represents the right- and left-side arm--hand actions as individual action tokens and organizes them into an interleaved sequence, explicitly exposing the two sides within the action sequence. To explicitly encode hand identity and temporal synchronization in this interleaved representation, a learnable hand-identity embedding distinguishes the two sides, while sequence--control-timestep factorized rotary positional encoding (RoPE) separates sequence position from control timestep, allowing actions at the same control timestep to share a temporal coordinate while retaining distinct sequence positions. Across all five bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks in DexJoCo, Coordi-$π$ achieves state-of-the-art performance under both \textit{rand-obj} and \textit{rand-full}, improving the average success rate over $π_{0.5}$ from 31.9\% to 51.3\% and from 18.3\% to 32.3\%, respectively. Coordi-$π$ also consistently outperforms $π_{0.5}$ across four real-world bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks.

papers.title: Beyond Reachability: A Relation-Semantic Reasoning Framework for Biomedical Multi-hop QA
papers.abstract: Biomedical multi-hop reasoning over knowledge graphs requires identifying a semantically valid relation sequence that supports the answer. Existing methods can retrieve correct answers, yet often rank them poorly within a large pool of seemingly relevant candidates. Even when a correct answer is retrieved, its associated evidence and reasoning path may fail to support the relation composition required by the question. We term this disconnect between answer reachability and evidential validity the reachable-but-invalid problem. We present ReSemReason, which shares a question-induced distribution over typed, directed relation schemas between candidate discovery and evidence selection. Schema compatibility guides graph search; ReSemAttn then uses relation-conditioned key/value projections and an uncertainty-weighted path prior to attend to candidate-specific evidence. A separate absolute-support score complements normalized attention when all retrieved paths are weak. The reported experiments on BioHopR, PrimeKGQA, and MedReason show improvements in answer ranking and answer-set quality. Path-discrimination analyses examine the distinction between endpoint correctness and evidential support. We also specify matched controls for search, attention, and schema uncertainty.

papers.title: Prefixes of Coxeter elements are Coxeter elements of the reflection subgroups they generate
papers.abstract: Let $(W,S)$ be a Coxeter system of finite rank, let $T$ be its set of reflections and let $c \in W$ be a Coxeter element.
