In their $L^2-$homology theory of von Neumann algebras, Connes and Shlyakhtenko defined a certain quantity, $0 \leq Δ(Ξ) \leq d$, as the Murray-von Neumann co-dimension of the Hilbert module generated by all $d-$tuples of finite rank operators obeying the above commutator condition with $Ξ\in \mathfrak{M} ^{1\times d}$. As demonstrated by Mai, Speicher and Yin, this $Δ$ measures, in a certain precise sense, the algebraic independence of the components of $Ξ$. Connes-Shlyakhtenko proved that $Δ$ is an upper bound for Voiculescu's non-microstates free entropy dimension, $δ^* (Ξ)$, and remark that it is of interest to determine whether these two quantities are equal. Using non-commutative function theory, we show that this is generally not the case, by constructing a triple of self-adjoint operators, $Ξ= (Ξ_1,Ξ_2,Ξ_3)$, for which this inequality is strict, $δ^*(Ξ) < Δ(Ξ)$.

papers.title: Zhang twists for semigroups and groupoids, with applications to Steinberg algebras
papers.abstract: Zhang twists provide a powerful mechanism for deforming graded algebras, while preserving their graded module categories. We extend this theory by introducing Zhang twists for graded semigroups and graded ample groupoids. We show that the twisting construction preserves a broad class of semigroup structures, and that two graded monoids are twists of each other if and only if their categories of graded sets are pointedly equivalent. We show that Zhang twists are compatible with noncommutative Stone duality: twists on graded-Boolean inverse semigroups are in correspondence with those on the associated graded ample groupoids. Moreover, in the setting of Steinberg algebras we prove that twisting the groupoid gives the same result as twisting the corresponding algebra. These results provide a unified framework linking graded semigroups, inverse semigroup duality, ample groupoids, and graded algebras, while extending the scope of Zhang twists to settings arising from symbolic dynamics, graph algebras, and Steinberg algebras.

papers.title: Can LLMs Anticipate Their Cruxes?
papers.abstract: To use language models to help us make decisions we would like to understand the rationale behind the language model's outputs. In principle, the language model provides its rationale as part of its text output. However, the sheer volume of text makes this hard to use in practice. In this paper, we are interested in extracting the cruxes that lead a model to recommend one action over another. We take a crux to be a sub-question that a model's rollouts disagree on, where changing its value may have altered the conclusion. A crux is therefore a property of the distribution of a model's rollouts, not of any one rollout. We consider three strategies of increasing computational cost. First, we just ask a model to identify, a priori, what the cruxes of a decision will be. Second, we have the model actually go through the process of generating a response and then extract the cruxes that arose in its reasoning. Finally, we generate many responses and extract the cruxes by comparing the reasoning across the rollouts. We make this last procedure computationally tractable with cheap calls to a reranker, an estimated 86 times less compute than a judge. We then conduct an extensive empirical evaluation to assess whether the computationally inexpensive options are sufficient. They are not. Across domains and models, we find that a model's a priori assessment of the cruxes has little relation to the factors that are actually identified as important a posteriori. Using a single rollout helps, but is still inadequate for identifying the full set of cruxes. Accordingly, for high-stakes decisions (and to understand the space of language model decision making) the many rollout procedure is unavoidable.

papers.title: Mind the Tail: Data Selection Through Sparse Concepts
papers.abstract: Data selection reallocates training support across visual concepts, including objects, attributes, color, texture, and backgrounds. Different allocation strategies may produce varied downstream model behavior, especially for tail concepts supported by only a few samples. Discarding them can hurt test-time robustness, while overemphasizing samples lying on category boundaries may introduce unstable training signals. This work explicitly investigates this relationship across fine-grained, spurious-correlation, and general image classification, as well as multimodal pretraining. Specifically, we use sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to extract concept activations from individual images. During selection, we accumulate the dataset-level concept support for each added sample. Applying diminishing returns to this distribution down-weights well-represented concepts and shifts the focus to the distribution tail. We then incorporate local support to find samples that reliably strengthen under-supported concepts. Empirical results show consistent improvements over strong data selection baselines across all benchmarks. We also reveal the connection between concepts our method enhances and the induced behavioral changes, including improved robustness against out-of-distribution and spurious contexts. This work establishes concept support, beyond individual sample importance, as a useful principle for data-efficient and robust learning.

papers.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for HPC Job Scheduling: A Statistical Evaluation
papers.abstract: Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) offers learned job selection for High-Performance Computing (HPC), but performance against heuristics alone does not establish value beyond action masking. Six DRL treatments are compared: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), Advantage Actor-Critic (A2C), and Deep Q-Network (DQN), each with and without masking. Three heuristics and a seed-paired masked uniform random control provide baselines across ten seeds on two real Slurm (Simple Linux Utility for Resource Management) workload traces, one homogeneous and one heterogeneous, under a common non-parametric framework. All masked treatments complete evaluation, whereas unmasked treatments are truncated. On the homogeneous trace, no masked DRL treatment significantly improves average waiting time or average and maximum bounded slowdown over the control. On the heterogeneous trace, MaskablePPO improves all three metrics relative to the control. Its average waiting time is equivalent to that of the three heuristics within a 10% margin, and its maximum bounded slowdown is 22% lower than that of Last-Come, First-Served (LCFS). MaskablePPO has the leading average waiting-time rank among complete treatments on both traces, but Nemenyi comparisons detect no significant difference from MaskableA2C. Among masked variants, MaskablePPO has the lowest recorded mean training time, while MaskableDQN has the lowest mean decision latency. These findings distinguish completion from baseline-specific scheduling gains and support including a masked random control when assessing the value of learned selection.

papers.title: Length control for foliations by Jordan curves via smooth quasiconformal maps
papers.abstract: Let $Ω\subsetneq\mathbb C$ be a non-empty simply connected domain and $0<p<2$. Bouchala and Koskela [Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. (2024)] proved that there exists a quasiconformal map $f:\mathbb D\toΩ$ such that $\int_0^1\ell(f(r S^1))^p\,dr<\infty$, and asked whether this conclusion holds at $p=2$, or even for every $0<p<2+\varepsilon$ with some $\varepsilon>0$. We answer this question affirmatively with $\varepsilon=2/157$ by constructing a single smooth $5$-quasiconformal map $f:\mathbb D\toΩ$ satisfying this integrability condition simultaneously for every $0<p<2+2/157$.

papers.title: Operator Algebraic Quantum Hypergroups
papers.abstract: We develop a theory of operator algebraic quantum hypergroups and their representations, formulated using a special case of the algebraic quantum hypergroup framework of van Daele and Delvaux. As part of the axioms, every operator algebraic quantum hypergroup admits a dual object of the same type. We prove that a certain universal completion in the compact case satisfies the axioms of an earlier notion of a compact quantum hypergroup in the sense of the second author and Chapovsky. As part of this theory, we discuss their (co)amenability properties. We consider examples induced by conditional expectations of algebraic quantum groups satisfying certain properties, which include quantum hypergroups corresponding to double cosets and automorphisms of quantum groups, and quantum hypergroups induced by representation categories of Kac type compact quantum groups.

papers.title: Audio-Visual Dog Identification and Tracking in Real-World Videos
papers.abstract: Identifying individual dogs from barks in real-world videos remains challenging and largely unexplored. Solving this problem would enable long-term behavioral analysis, veterinary monitoring, and animal welfare monitoring by attributing vocalizations and behaviors to the correct individual. Real-world videos are challenging because multiple dogs may bark simultaneously, become occluded, or move in and out of view. Prior studies show that canine vocalizations and visual appearance contain discriminative identity information, but these modalities have largely been studied independently. We present a multimodal dog-fingerprinting framework combining visual identification, multiple-object tracking, and canine vocal fingerprinting to associate bark events with individual dogs while maintaining persistent profiles. The framework synchronizes bark events with tracked dogs and updates profiles using visual appearance and vocal characteristics, enabling identification despite occlusion, overlapping vocalizations, and off-screen barking. We also introduce a benchmark of 46 real-world videos containing 213 manually annotated bark events. Our framework correctly localizes the active visible dog in 61.83% of visible events at IoU $\geq 0.30$ and achieves a 91.33% F1 score for visible versus off-screen barking detection.

papers.title: Variable Masking for Climate Emulation in ACE
papers.abstract: In the recent AI Model Intercomparison Project (AIMIP) benchmark, the ACE2.1-ERA5 emulator was shown to underestimate the true near-surface warming trend both during the training period and the out-of-sample extrapolation period. In this work, we present M-ACE2S (Masked-ACE2S), a modified version of the stochastic ACE2S model, which uses variable masking during training and reduces the reliance of M-ACE2S on any single input channel. We show that M-ACE2S improves long-term near-surface air temperature prediction. We also present a novel data normalization strategy called "global mean removal", which, combined with masking, further improves the near-surface temperature forecasts. We show that M-ACE2S outperforms the ACE2S baseline on in-sample data for ERA5 while improving training stability and generalizability of near-surface temperature to unseen forcing when paired with global mean removal.

papers.title: LWM-TF: A Wireless Foundation Model on 5G NR Time-Frequency Resource Grids
papers.abstract: Received OFDM grids preserve both pilot and payload observations, yet wireless foundation models are rarely pre-trained on them. We introduce LWM-TF, a 9.58M-parameter factorized masked autoencoder pre-trained on complex 5G NR uplink grids taken after the FFT and before channel estimation. Each block attends first across OFDM symbols and then across resource blocks and receive antennas, and the mask follows the same two axes. Because the payload phase is unpredictable, the model reconstructs the normalized log-power of each masked token and predicts its scale separately; ablations show that the two terms are complementary and that this target outperforms complex-signal reconstruction. The encoder is pre-trained on 850,496 physical uplink shared channel (PUSCH) slots from a 10^6-slot dataset simulated with the NR transmit chain under various channel conditions. With the encoder frozen, linear probes classify modulation, predict CRC success, and detect UE mobility. On a separately generated test set, 16 labeled slots per class give 0.85 modulation accuracy, 0.82 CRC area under the ROC curve (AUROC), and 0.73 mobility AUROC, ahead of a supervised CNN on every paired draw. With 10,000 labels the probes reach 0.94, 0.96, and 0.92, well above engineered receiver statistics, and detect mobility where the CNN stays at chance. Without any impairment labels, distances in the frozen feature space flag unseen waveform impairments with 0.78 macro AUROC, against 0.68 for receiver statistics. A single pre-trained encoder thus provides receiver features that transfer across tasks, most strongly when labels are scarce.

papers.title: Measure Theory in Convergence Spaces Part II: Abstract Integration in Net Convergence Structures
papers.abstract: The construction of a coherent and general integration procedure is the central question of this second part of our study of measure theory in convergence spaces. We define, and establish convergence theorems for such process of integration, called the net Riemann integration, in convergence groups and commutative monoids, preserving the prescribed convergence throughout. The underlying interchange theorem admits noncommutative groups and requires right completeness only at the cardinality of the error family. Under intrinsic stability assumptions, countable error control therefore needs only sequential completeness, even for arbitrary integration nets, from which we also stablish a general version of Henstock's lemma. The resulting uniform theorems reaches incomplete ranges in which no complete subspace contains a tail of the approximating integrals. In the ordered locally solid convergence theory side, countability of the inner direction replaces countable accessibility of the approximants, and local existence arguments yield monotone and dominated convergence and, under additional controller assumptions, a further extension through increasing integrable barriers with pointwise coverage and uniformly vanishing excess primitives. This constructs the limiting integral without a common integrable envelope and gives uniform control of primitive variation. We finish with two appendices on new and general results of abstract metrization of net convergences and related topics.

papers.title: MASON: Materials Atomistic Structure builder Operated in Natural language
papers.abstract: Building reliable atomistic models is a critical and often challenging step in first-principles calculations. Although large language model agents can assist with structure generation, they lack direct capabilities for crystallographic operations and therefore struggle to construct complex structures reliably. Here we present MASON, an AI-native toolkit for atomistic structure construction that can be invoked by agents through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). In an end-to-end example, an agent builds a CO/Pt(111) adsorption model from a natural language request. By equipping agents with dedicated structure-building tools, MASON enables reliable and efficient atomistic model construction and provides a foundation for autonomous first-principles workflows.

papers.title: CausalEvo: Causal Skill Self-Evolution for Health LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents for health can accumulate reusable textual skills from task feedback, such as calculation criteria, measurement time points, and formula units. Deciding which skills to retain is consequential: useful rules improve later answers, while faulty generalizations propagate errors. We propose CausalEvo, a method for causal skill self-evolution that estimates the relative effects of deliberately changed skill sets while holding the model weights, feedback cases, and rule count fixed. At each evolution step, a frozen LLM proposes candidate rules, which are pooled with the incumbent skills so that the current skill set remains a feasible choice. Paired skill replacements against shared background rules are scored on the same feedback cases; least squares converts the score differences into relative skill values, and the top-ranked rules are retained, favoring incumbents on ties. A decision-loss bound separates candidate support, approximation, and estimation errors. On six MedCalc-Bench-Verified tasks with 120 held-out cases, CausalEvo achieves 60.00% accuracy, compared with 55.83% for SkillOpt and 51.67% without skills. Across the recorded training configurations, which use different optimization budgets, it consumes 55.6% fewer training tokens than SkillOpt. Gains concentrate in particular calculations alongside regressions on others, and paired accuracy intervals include zero. CausalEvo turns task feedback into controlled decisions about skill retention and replacement. Project repository: https://github.com/txbrook/CausalEvo

papers.title: Crossing numbers of simplicial complexes
papers.abstract: This paper studies crossing numbers of $d$-dimensional simplicial complexes drawn in $\mathbb R^{2d}$ or $\mathbb S^{2d}$. We clarify and generalize a number of known results and conjectures from the graph case to higher dimensions: the crossing lemma (including the exceptional case of two-dimensional complexes drawn in dimension $4$), a generalized Harary-Hill conjecture (and evidence for it), existence of a midrange crossing constant (in a weak sense), and upper bound constructions based on stochastic geometry (related to Sylvester's problem) and the cyclic polytope. Some of our results are new even in the case of graphs: we give a simple proof of the Harary-Hill conjecture for antipodal drawings, and sharpen the threshold above which the rectilinear and spherical crossing numbers of the Erdős-Rényi random graph behave like those of the complete graph.

papers.title: Failure Is the Mother of Success: Recovering Supervision with Grounding Hindsight
papers.abstract: When every rollout for a problem fails, GRPO receives neither a successful exemplar nor a nonzero group-relative advantage, so it learns nothing from exactly the problems it most needs to learn. The failed reasoning can nevertheless suggest what to try next. We present Replay-Selected Hindsight Distillation (RSHD), which turns failed attempts into an additional, tested source of supervision during GRPO training. The policy writes a corrective note about each failed attempt without seeing a reference answer or solution, then re-solves the problem with the note in context. A note is admitted only if its replays succeed more often than the original group did, after screening for notes that state the answer, and an admitted replay is distilled into the plain-prompt policy. Because admission is decided by fresh successes rather than by the failed rollout itself, the procedure can recover supervision from groups in which every attempt failed, and it applies equally to failures in mixed groups. Only the policy is trained, the only judge is the outcome verifier, and deployment requires no notes or extra inference. Across model families and sizes and two training domains, RSHD consistently improves over GRPO on in-domain benchmarks, and the gains carry over to out-of-domain evaluation sets.

papers.title: Testing Tail-Index Homogeneity via Exceedance-Covariate Independence
papers.abstract: We propose a test of whether the tail index of a heavy-tailed outcome is homogeneous across observed covariates. The key observation is that, under tail-index homogeneity, normalized log exceedances are asymptotically independent of the covariates even when tail frequencies vary with them. This leads to a simple-to-implement permutation test based on distance covariance, without estimating conditional tail indices or specifying the form of tail-index heterogeneity. For the global and locally balanced versions, we establish validity for order-statistic thresholds and give conditions for consistency and local power. Local balancing selects extremes within two covariate groups and can improve power when tail selection concentrates the covariates. Simulations illustrate these gains. In French motor insurance data, upper conditional quantiles vary with risk characteristics, but the tail-index tests do not reject a common tail index.

papers.title: Deep Learning for Forest Plantation Mapping in Godavari Districts of Andhra Pradesh, India
papers.abstract: Small-area forest plantations play a vital role in the socioeconomic well-being of farmers in Southeast Asia. Most plantations are established on former agricultural land, often on land less suitable for agriculture. Plantations that are converted from natural forest have adverse impacts on biodiversity. Mapping small-area plantations is thus important to understand the dynamics of forest cover in Southeast Asia and to study the social, economic, and ecological effects of this important land cover and land use change. While the small size of forest plantations makes it difficult to detect them using moderate resolution satellite sensors, the problem is exacerbated by the high degree of mixing between plantations, surrounding vegetation, and other land covers, which often show variegated responses in satellite signals across space and time. In this paper, we study the problem of mapping small-area forest plantations in East and West Godavari districts of Andhra Pradesh, India using deep learning methods. Remotely sensed cloud-free data from the Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 S10 product were classified using a pixel-level neural network and training data labeled using a field-based survey in concert with expert aerial photo interpretation. We compare the performance of deep learning methods with a baseline random forest classifier in our study region of 21543 sq. km over a period of 3 years and analyze the differences in the results across land cover classes and seasons.

papers.title: Acceleration and its Limits in Gaussian Variational Inference
papers.abstract: We study whether the classical momentum-based acceleration that improves the condition-number dependence of gradient descent from $κ$ to $\sqrtκ$ for strongly convex, smooth objectives extends to Gaussian variational inference (GVI) for strongly log-concave, log-smooth target distributions. With exact Gaussian expectations, a convex composite formulation of GVI yields the classical accelerated $\sqrtκ$ convergence rate. However, when only pointwise derivatives are available, we construct a family of strongly log-concave targets for which any randomized algorithm requires $κ^{1-o(1)}$ queries to achieve a fixed objective accuracy, even when the initial objective gap is bounded independently of $κ$. Thus curvature bounds alone cannot guarantee uniform accelerated total-query complexity. We then ask which additional structure permits acceleration and give positive examples: under a Hessian-Lipschitz assumption, variance-reduced stochastic methods yield accelerated guarantees when the Hessian variation is sufficiently small. Finally, experiments on real datasets show substantial empirical speedups from acceleration across a broad range of methods.

papers.title: GeoMix: A Bayesian Framework for Stratigraphic and Geotechnical Inference
papers.abstract: Accurate characterisation of subsea sediments is essential for engineering projects such as offshore wind farms, but the challenging environment and large spatial domains involved make dense geotechnical measurements impractical. Seismic traces offer a cheap, abundant complement, yet their geotechnical interpretation relies on subjective judgement, leading to biased, hard-to-validate predictions of sediment structure. To address this, we introduce GeoMix, a fully Bayesian hierarchical framework for jointly inferring geological stratigraphy and geotechnical properties from seismic and geotechnical data. GeoMix uses a Potts Markov random field to represent spatially coherent geology organised into distinct stratigraphic layers. Labels derived from seismic interpretation are linked to the latent stratigraphy through an observation model that captures elevated uncertainty near transitions between strata. Conditional on the latent stratigraphy, geotechnical properties are modelled using class-specific Gaussian processes, with scalable likelihood evaluation enabled by a grouped Vecchia approximation. Together, these components yield a unified latent-variable model capable of recovering stratigraphy, quantifying uncertainty, and predicting geotechnical properties across large three-dimensional domains. Simulation studies and an application to the IJmuiden Ver offshore wind farm show that GeoMix produces spatially coherent stratigraphic estimates and sediment predictions that are better calibrated and more accurate than existing approaches.

papers.title: From Individual Songs to Music Corpora: Evaluating Explainable Harmonic Decision-Making on HookTheory
papers.abstract: Automatic melody harmonization is often evaluated through individual compositions or data-driven corpus models. This study examines whether an explainable harmonic decision model developed for individual songs can be applied to independently collected human annotations without changing its rules. We evaluate a frozen Explainable Melody Harmonizer (EMH) on selected HookTheory excerpts containing aligned melody and chord annotations. EMH generates chord sequences from melody alone using explicit criteria for melodic compatibility, harmonic function, persistence, cadence, meter-aware segmentation, and Viterbi-like optimization. Human chords are withheld during generation and used only for post-hoc comparison. Nineteen excerpts yielded 439 evaluable harmonic segments. Exact chord agreement reached 20.50%, chord-root agreement 31.66%, and harmonic-function agreement 47.62%, with functions assessed relative to the key inferred by EMH. Decision-level analysis identified 203 segments (46.24%) where the human chord lay outside the model's candidate vocabulary and 146 (33.26%) where it was available but not selected. These findings distinguish representational limitations from differences in chord selection without treating the human reference as the only musically valid solution. The study demonstrates a reproducible, interpretable approach to corpus-based evaluation of harmonic decision-making.

papers.title: A Bayesian hierarchical push-forward method for cluster Randomized Controlled Trial power calculations in complex humanitarian settings
papers.abstract: The design and evaluation of public health interventions in humanitarian crises demand rigorous yet flexible methodological approaches. Cluster-randomized controlled trials (cRCTs) are increasingly used to generate evidence in such settings, but trial conduct is frequently complicated by displacement, resource constraints, and cluster dropout. Although Bayesian methods provide a natural framework for hierarchical modeling, probabilistic uncertainty quantification, and the integration of prior knowledge, their use in cRCT design remains limited, particularly with respect to anticipating missingness. This paper introduces a Bayesian design strategy tailored for cRCTs in complex settings, motivated by a forthcoming trial in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh, that will assess a community health worker adherence intervention for cardiovascular disease and hepatitis C. Our approach incorporates prior information on cluster and individual-level dropout into power and sample size calculations via a hierarchical model and push-forward distribution framework. Through simulation studies, we evaluate the performance of the proposed method under varying levels of missingness and correlation structures. The approach is then applied to inform the design of the Bangladesh trial. We disseminate our methods via a publicly-available R Shiny app to promote accessibility and usability to investigators. By formalizing Bayesian strategies that anticipate data loss, this work provides a foundation for more robust and efficient cRCTs in humanitarian contexts; therefore, strengthening the evidence base for health interventions in resource-limited and crisis-affected populations.

papers.title: Beyond Match Results: Bayesian Mediation of Ability, Performance, and Winning in Professional Tennis
papers.abstract: Match results measure competitive ability, but they do not explain how ability is expressed during play. Match statistics offer a natural mediator, however performance is usually measured over the same match as the outcome: a full-match statistic uses events that help determine the winner, while a first-set statistic is earlier but rests on fewer service points and still contributes to the result. Comparing the two therefore mixes timing and precision. We develop a Bayesian mediation framework for this problem. Dynamic abilities on hard, clay, and grass courts are estimated from previous seasons only and are linked to both players' service performance, and a Bradley--Terry model relates ability and performance to the match result. A control mediator samples the first set's number of service points from the full match, separating the measurement window from the point count. In 3,820 men's matches, the hard-court mediated share rises from 0.52 with a first-set mediator to 0.95 with a full-match mediator; the point-count contrast accounts for 0.30 of this gap and the window contrast for 0.13. The pattern replicates on the women's tour. Simulations and sensitivity analyzes examine the decomposition and assumptions needed for a causal interpretation.

papers.title: Stationarity equations for fractional affine area measures: ellipsoid rigidity and polytopal solutions
papers.abstract: Xi and Zhao established a first variation formula for affine inequalities involving radial mean bodies, and asked two geometric questions about the resulting stationarity equation: whether the bodies already known to satisfy it are the only ones, and whether its smooth solutions are exactly the ellipsoids. We answer both. Every strictly convex solution of the equation with $q>-1$, $q\ne0,n$ is an ellipsoid, which answers the second question affirmatively while replacing smoothness and everywhere positive Gauss curvature by strict convexity. Every full-dimensional facet-transitive polytope satisfies the equation, and so does the polar of every vertex-transitive polytope with respect to its volume centroid; the rhombic dodecahedron, the thirteen Catalan solids and the bipyramids over regular polygons other than the octahedron provide infinitely many affinely inequivalent solutions that are not affine images of regular polytopes or balls, so the answer to the first question is negative. The rigidity proof compares overlap integrals along a continuous Steiner path: stationarity forces an increase of order $o(t)$, whereas a nonaffine chord midpoint function forces an increase of order $t$. For negative parameters the required comparison rests on a minimization formula over bounded measurable auxiliary sets.

papers.title: Learning to Read Out: Unembedding Dynamics in Language Model Pretraining
papers.abstract: When does a language model acquire a capability? Developmental studies usually answer this by tracking when models start producing the correct token. But that prediction passes through the unembedding matrix, or readout, which is itself still being learned during pretraining. We show that a model's hidden states can encode task information before its own readout expresses it, so timelines read from outputs conflate what the model encodes with what its readout expresses. To track the readout directly, we introduce parameter-trajectory crosscoding, which fits one sparse dictionary to every token's readout row at every checkpoint. Unlike crosscoders on activations, it needs only checkpoint weights. We use it to locate a narrow early window, 0.4-1.1% of the way through Pythia's pretraining, in which the readout reorganizes and WordNet word categories become decodable from its rows. By then, linear probes on the hidden states already decode task information that the model's own outputs do not yet show. To test whether such gaps depend on how fast the readout learns, we pretrain small models from scratch that differ only in the readout's learning rate. We find that raising it makes the readout develop earlier and the gap close sooner, with little effect on final loss. Together, these results imply that early in training, where many developmental transitions are dated, a behavioral date can reflect when the readout learns to express task information and not when the model learns it.

papers.title: On the Last-Iterate Convergence of Clipped Gradient Methods
papers.abstract: In stochastic (strongly) convex optimization, establishing last-iterate convergence guarantees for first-order methods has recently garnered increasing attention, as this not only deepens the theoretical understanding of these algorithms but also aligns more closely with practice. Notably, people have demonstrated that one of the most famous, simple, and popular methods, Stochastic Gradient Descent ($\mathtt{SGD}$), provably achieves last-iterate convergence. However, the existing results may have limited applicability, since they typically rely on strong conditions on the gradient noise (e.g., an exponentially decaying tail) rather than the more realistic heavy-tailed noise. Unfortunately, when faced with heavy-tailed noise, $\mathtt{SGD}$ is known to exhibit undesirable behavior or even fail to converge. To address the challenge of heavy-tailed noise, people have proposed $\mathtt{Clipped}\text{-}\mathtt{SGD}$, an algorithm that combines $\mathtt{SGD}$ with a simple mechanism, gradient clipping. Although $\mathtt{Clipped}\text{-}\mathtt{SGD}$ performs well in practice, its last-iterate convergence property remains highly underexplored. In this work, we prove the first optimal last-iterate rates in high probability for $\mathtt{Clipped}\text{-}\mathtt{SGD}$ under heavy-tailed noise, thereby closing a gap in the literature.

papers.title: Localized high-Q resonances enable electrically defined beam steering in lithium niobate metasurfaces
papers.abstract: High-speed beam steering for LiDAR and optical communication requires independent, reconfigurable control of optical phase. We demonstrate a metasurface combining lithium niobate's Pockels effect with high-Q (Q > 1700) silicon guided-mode resonance nanoantennas whose localized resonances allow individual electro-optic control at a 1 $μ$m pitch. Identical arrays steer light to 53.5$^\circ$ or 32.4$^\circ$, with the angle set by the bias pattern rather than antenna geometry. We measure 18.0% 0th-order modulation depth, 0.09% of incident power in the steered order, and a 940 MHz detected modulation bandwidth. Mode-overlap analysis shows how inter-element coupling limits usable Q, providing design rules for compact, high-speed beam steering.
